speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was talking about the two major errors contained in the statement of the minister of immigration of October 4, 1991 regarding the refugee backlog clearance program.
The second error is that the backlog will not be completed within its original budget. The original budget as announced by the former minister when the program began was $100 million. Now it is $179 million and the minister pretends it is within budget.
The program for clearing the backlog is nothing more than smoke and mirrors. It is a cross between amnesty and administrative review pretending to be a program to ferret out bogus refugees. The program is neither on time nor on budget.
Refugee claimants whose lives have been on hold for as long as four years are now being told by this minister that they will have to wait an additional 15 months. Despite this, the minister said: "The program is meeting its objective to clear these claims in a fair and humanitarian manner".
Mr. Speaker, there is nothing fair or humanitarian about waiting up to five years to have one's claim heard.

Mr. Speaker, for some time now, and especially during Small
Business Week, workers at Donohue Matane and their socio-economic partners in the Gaspe have been vigorously pursuing efforts to start operations again at their ultra modern plant and obtain the paper machine they need to upgrade the value of their natural resources.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke personally to the Prime Minister, and I know he is giving this matter special attention.
I therefore wish to take this opportunity to again invite the Prime Minister and the Minister for International Trade to continue their efforts to find a potential investor who will help meet the expectations of workers at the Matane pulp mill.
Mr. Prime Minister, the people of the Gaspe are counting on your support.

Mr. Speaker, we are once again seeing the attempt to misuse the cancertreating drug depo-provera as a contraceptive.
The chief of the Baffin Regional Health Board in the Northwest Territories is quoted today as saying that depo-provera is being offered to northern Inuit women as a contraceptive despite having never been approved by the federal government for such use.
Indeed, the drug has been subject to an intense campaign by Canadian women and health groups to ensure that it is not used as a contraceptive because of well documented concerns about breast cancer, foetal abnormalities, and more than 20 side effects.
To his credit the former minister of health, Jake Epp, disallowed the use of the drug as a contraceptive because of concerns about the long-term safety of women. I call upon the current minister of health to review the drug approval process so that legal drugs cannot be misused and so that these Inuit women are not put at risk.

Mr. Speaker, today I wish to pay tribute to the remarkable performance of nine members of the Judo Club of Bois-des-Fi-lion, a municipality in my riding. Several days ago, they won seven medals, including two gold, at the International Judo Championship in Newark, New Jersey.
Both athletes and trainers have shown that with hard work and determination, and despite limited financial means, they were able to achieve the highest levels of excellence.
These young people are worthy representatives of the riding of Terrebonne, the town of Bois-des-Filion and this country, and we are all very proud of them. I urge them to keep up the good work, and I can assure them that we are all very proud of their performance and their success.
Once again, three cheers and congratulations! We are all very proud of you.

Mr. Speaker, I have received a petition signed by over 1,400 constituents concerning government initiatives to close or cut services at the postal outlets at Drake Pharmacy in Windsor Park in my constituency.
These cuts and closures have also been imposed on other facilities, for example, McCulluogh Drugs, Marion Grocery, and Metro Drugs. Over the years staff in the post offices in St. Boniface and Norwood have been reduced as well.
These cuts and closings are all in addition to the annoyance they have suffered with supermailboxes, astronomical increases in postal rates, including the GST on stamps and other services, inadequate postal service for certain regions of the constituency, for example River Park South and St. Vital.
This government is inconveniencing and really putting out all constituents, particularly business people, seniors, and handicapped residents.
When will this government have a fair, comprehensive and accessible postal service for all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, 180 residents in the Abitibi area will meet at the Chateau d'Amos on November 1 and 2 to identify mechanisms that apply the co-operative principle and are most likely to meet the needs of the community. They will do so within the framework of a regional seminar held by the co-operative assembly.
The general theme of this assembly will be how to achieve quality development together. Regional members of the co-operative movement and their socio-economic partners will have discussions on two of three subjects on the agenda: community development using the co-operative formula; co-operative education; and inter-co-operation.
According to Mr. Ferland Miron, president of the Seminar's Organizing Committee and director of the Serres cooperatives de Guyenne, it was and is up to co-operators and their partners to work together to achieve quality development, because it is undeniably true that co-operatives can increase their contribution to the region's economic development and, by using their formula, promote development of individual potential.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute and to inform the House of the tragic death of one of the great leaders of the Yukon native community, Mr. Elijah Smith.
In 1973, it was Mr. Smith who travelled to Ottawa to begin Yukon land claims discussions. In Mr. Smith's hands was the document Together Today for our Children Tomorrow. It was a precedent setting paper and served as a model for future discussions between federal governments and aboriginal people.
October 23, 1991

Mr. Smith was a great man, one of those rare people who could unite others on the strength of his vision. His eloquence and activism on behalf of his people and his commitment to Canada and the democratic process were renown.
Mr. Smith so loved his country that he served in the Second World War and lost his Indian status as a result of doing so. But his love for his own people was no less. In the hope of bettering their lives, he founded the Yukon Native Brotherhood and was later instrumental in bringing together all of the aboriginal people in the Yukon.
With aboriginal and non-aboriginal people in the Yukon, Mr. Smith has been a true leader. He will be truly missed.
I want to say to Mr. Smith's family, and I am sure I echo the sentiments of all members of this House, that a great leader has been lost to us but that his memory will go on.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Pembroke, Ontario, a large host of Canadians from all walks of life gathered in St. Columbkille's Cathedral to celebrate the gift of the heroic life and death of Sister Claire Hass who was murdered last week while performing her dedicated missionary work in the Bahamas.
Sister Claire grew up within the peaceful, hardworking, farm community of Admaston township in the county of Renfrew. She entered the Grey Sisters Community in Pembroke, Ontario, in 1947 and began a long career of religious service; nursing and teaching included.
Her missionary work took place in many parts of the world. The most important aspect about Sister Claire was the fact that she was representative of that era in Canadian history which saw many very dedicated, idealistic and realistic young people go from the farmlands and the streets of our wonderful nation to serve their Maker by helping those who could not help themselves.
Her "halls of fame" were the streets of the poor and helpless, her classroom was her castle, her loving care wherever she was needed was her hospital. She practised
her missionary work with conviction and purpose. Her life's work is an example for many Canadians to follow.
There is no doubt in the minds of those of us who knew her that Sister Claire Hass was welcomed into heaven with the words: "Well done thy good and faithful servant".

Mr. Speaker, during Small Business Week, I would like to pay tribute to Canada's small businesses, especially those in the riding of Joliette which I have the honour to represent.
Small businesses are the engines of Canada's economy-no one can deny that. We realize they represent over 97 per cent of Canadian businesses and that their annual sales generate over $326 billion.
Joliette has many small businesses which, through hard work and determination, have managed to carve out a niche in a market that is becoming increasingly competitive, both nationally and internationally. Two examples are Les Ateliers d'usinage M.D.M. Inc. and Filochrome Inc., and there are many more.
Mr. Speaker, Canada's prosperity depends on the prosperity of small businesses. That is why since 1984, the federal government has been trying to create an economic climate that is favourable to small business growth and development.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister for Science announced the names of 3,200 new Canada scholars for 1991-92. Thirteen of these scholars are from the federal riding of Peterborough. These 3,200 new Canada scholars are joining the ranks of more than
4,000	established Canada scholars who are already pursuing studies in mathematics, engineering and natural sciences.
Canada Scholarships are worth $2,000 annually and can be renewed up to three times for a total value of $8,000 to each student. A Canada Scholarship holds more than monetary rewards, it brings prestige, recognition and career opportunities to the recipients. The Canadian government has pledged $80 million to this scholarship program.
Today's Canada scholars are tomorrow's scientists and engineers. I would like to take this opportunity to extend congratulations to both new and continuing Canada scholars. I wish them every success in meeting the challenge of being a Canada scholar.

Mr. Speaker, over the last 30 years, Quebecers have built a society based on respect for others. They are proud of it. Today, they are disappointed, and for a good reason. During the Oka crisis, people in English Canada and abroad took the opportunity to tarnish Quebec's image. Now, in the Great Whale issue, people are doing all they can to demolish Quebec's reputation. The most shameful part of this story, Mr. Speaker, is that those who sit in government and pretend to defend Quebec's interests in Ottawa remain silent. Every time Quebec's reputation is threatened, they keep quiet. Is there connivance in all that, Mr. Speaker? I really wonder today!

Mr. Speaker, on April 6, 1990, the governments of Canada and Quebec concluded an agreement to create the Saguenay-St. Lawrence marine park in the medium term. They thus laid the foundation for what promises to become such a major experiment in environmental protection that it will be among the most important ecological initiatives in the world.
All interested persons and groups in the community, especially Mr. Corbin, president of the marine park coalition, ask both governments to stop their bureaucratic quarreling and to involve the community in this important development for all of eastern Canada.
As the coalition points out, the Saguenay-St. Lawrence marine park is neither federal nor provincial but belongs to present and future generations. To attain the environmental objectives that led to creating this park, officials must stop their useless jurisdictional disputes and personal bickering and let Parks Canada share its expertise and financial resources with Quebec and our region.
Let us put an end to these ivory tower frustrations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday in the House, the Prime Minister said that he was not seeking the position of United Nations Secretary General. Given that statement, I ask the Deputy Prime Minister: Has the government asked Yves Fortier, our ambassador to the United Nations, to withdraw the Prime Minister's name from the list of candidates for that position, or has Mr. Fortier been asked to become the chief organizer for the Prime Minister's election campaign in New York?

Mr. Speaker, it would be very difficult to withdraw from something that you were not a party to or a a part of and so the answer is no.
October 23, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I took the Prime Minister at his word when he said that he was not-and I repeat-that he was not a candidate for the job in New York. I believed him. Now, 24 hours later, the Deputy Prime Minister cannot tell me why the name of the Prime Minister has not been withdrawn from this list. The Prime Minister cannot have it both ways. Either he wants the job or he does not want the job.
I would like to know from the Deputy Prime Minister: What kind of instructions has the government given to Ambassador Fortier and the 1,200 Canadian diplomats abroad? Are they campaigning abroad, speaking for Canada or trying to find a golden parachute for the Prime Minister?

speechtext:
Surely it is a reflection of the esteem and the regard with which he is held internationally, and surely it reflects the prominence and the importance of Canada in the leadership role and the activity it has been involved in since the United Nations started.
The fact of the matter is that the name was placed there by someone without the Prime Minister's consent. He has neither sought nor is seeking nor intends to seek such a position. As far as we are concerned, the matter is dead.

Oral Questions
said he was not interested and he was not going to take the job.
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister a question. One and a half million people in Canada are looking for jobs today. In Sault Ste. Marie, 20,000 people have joined together to save Algoma Steel. They are in the gallery today and they have presented a very good document to the government, and the government does not want to listen to them.
My question is very straightforward: When will the Prime Minister stop promoting himself for a job abroad and start promoting Canada-
The hon. minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President

I remind the hon. member that this government has already ploughed about $200 million plus into that facility, so we do have an interest in it.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
Canadians have a right to know what the government's policy is with respect to the question of filling what will soon be vacant post of Secretary-General of the United Nations. Canada will have to decide whether Canada, among possibilities, is going to support the placement of the first woman Secretary-General of the United Nations, the first Secretary-General from the continent of Africa, or whether Canada is looking for a bailout, a parachute for an unpopular Prime Minister here at home.

October 23, 1991
Oral Questions
We ask the Deputy Prime Minister: What instructions has the Government of Canada given to our ambassador at the UN, Yves Fortier, and to our ambassadors around the world? Have they been instructed to support the candidacy of the Prime Minister, or have they been given other instructions?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is worse than Trudeau and Iran.

It is not unreasonable for members of Parliament, indeed for the people of Canada, to ask the question whether or not the Prime Minister of this country has allowed his name to stand as a candidate for Secretary-General of the United Nations. It is perfectly reasonable to expect a straight answer. We have not had one.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister: Has the Prime Minister allowed his name to stand? We know it has not been withdrawn. Has Canada given instructions to our diplomatic personnel? It is not believable that we would show a benign interest in this.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs.
I am sure that while there are many things the minister and I might disagree with we do agree on one thing, and that is that we want to see the unity of Canada preserved and enhanced. We want to see the confederation of this country improved.
I want to raise with the minister some very serious concerns. I understand, and I understand well the process, that the constitutional joint parliamentary committee is not the minister's responsibility as such, that it is separate.
However, I want to ask the minister a question because this is a very serious issue of process. There were other alternatives to a kind of process we might use for the Constitution. The minister and his government wanted to see a joint parliamentary committee. We agreed to participate.
I want to say to the minister that there are serious concerns within the committee about consultation, about organization and about notice being given in the various regions of this country so that people who want to participate can.
Because of the extraordinary importance of this issue, will the minister make inquiries to ensure that the committee is truly functioning in a non-partisan and an organized manner so that all Canadians can have their say?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally, if the Leader of the New Democratic Party thinks that I should make inquiries, I will. I guess I will start with her and ask her to state directly what it is that concerns her. If there is a problem that she states directly, I will then try to deal with it.
October 23, 1991

I would hope that perhaps in the process she could indicate to me who are the three official members of the New Democratic Party serving on the committee.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
Yes, there are specific concerns if the minister would like me to raise them with him. There are concerns about the lack of notice for those members in provinces and territories who want to participate. We cannot have a participatory process if people do not know and cannot prepare for these. It is a very serious concern.
There are concerns about how contracts are being let in the committee, whether in fact those contracts are approved by the committee, and whether they are going through a proper process. There are concerns in the committee about whether in fact the committee is committed and the committee chair appointed by this government is committed-

I know that the hon. member for Yukon will realize that in asking questions about what is taking place in a committee there are some narrow constraints under our rules.
The hon. member for Yukon is expressing some concerns that may more properly be the object of a question to perhaps a committee chairperson. I think the matters the hon. member is raising go beyond what the minister could in fact answer because he would then be answering for the committee itself.

Mr. Speaker, I could phrase the question very succintly.
Will the minister ensure that Canadians have proper notice of the consultation process that is going to take place? Will he ensure that the committee itself is working in the non-partisan fashion in which he intended the committee to work?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly do everything within my power to ensure that. It would be helpful, in the interests of maintaining the respect for that committee which I think all members of Parliament, with perhaps some exceptions want it to enjoy, if there are specific concerns the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party has if she
Oral Questions
raised them with me directly, if they are mine to resolve, rather than waiting for Question Period in the House of Commons to do that.
She has my undertaking to do my best to maintain the effectiveness and the non-partisan nature of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I have a final supplementary question for the minister.
Again we share the minister's concern that this committee work fulfil the function it must do, if it is to have the confidence of the Canadian people.
One of the real concerns is that there have been a number of TV ads, information and 1-800 numbers at a fairly significant cost to the government. The committee is proposing to double the budget for advertising.
I want to ask the minister: What does he feel is an appropriate method of informing Canadians? Is it by doubling the budget of the committee-

The hon. member for Yukon, as I said earlier, may very well have questions that ought to be put to a committee chairperson.
I am constrained by the rules, as we all are, and I think that question goes beyond what can be put to the minister under the circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology-
Today the Community Action Team from Sault Ste. Marie met with the government to demand a commitment of support from the government to save thousands and thousands of jobs at Algoma Steel in Sault Ste. Marie, because in eight days' time the court protection from foreclosure runs out for this company.
The plan to restructure this company involves a buyout by the employees which requires a special tax incentive.
I wonder why the Government of Canada is refusing to provide a special tax incentive to help these employees carry out a buyout program and save these thousands and thousands of jobs. Can the minister explain why they are refusing that?

October 23, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to correct one thing. I believe it was one of the previous speakers from the Liberal side who said that we did not care about this issue. Nothing could be further from the truth.
Members of our caucus met with the group from Algoma yesterday and today and had quite full discussions with them. We have agreed on the areas where we do have a direct involvement. One of them is in relation to tax treatment on a buyout. Other areas would include training or early retirement for older employees.
These are matters that are under consideration in an active way. Members of my department have been meeting actively with people in the community, people from the company, Mr. Gaudry, the union and other interested parties, all with a view to putting together what is the most appropriate response to a very difficult situation.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question for the minister involves the restructuring of Algoma.
In the business plan that the company put forward it suggested that some $46.8 million would be required for industrial and employee adjustment programs, as well as a bridging pension program for older workers, to allow them to retire with some dignity.
I want to ask the minister, in going before the court next week, if the government prepared to give its commitment that it will provide that $46.8 million to assist these older employees who are facing the loss of their jobs and their livelihood.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in my earlier response, there is a range of issues under consideration here. They are all linked. There are different responsibilities for the Dominion Foundries Company, Algoma itself, the banks, the union, the provincial government and the federal government. There is a wide range of responsibilities here.
As I indicated to my hon. friend in my previous answer, these proposals are all under consideration. As soon as there is a proposal to put forward that all are happy with
then that is when we will have some very clear answers for him.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I want to ask the minister about major transfer payment cutbacks to the provinces and territories.
I would like to ask the minister about the reduction in growth of payments to the Northwest Territories by 9 per cent over the past six years.
How can the minister justify a reduction in transfer payments to the Northwest Territories by $110 million over five years when the majority of communities has a 50 per cent unemployment rate and the cost of living in some cases is 60 per cent higher than that of places like Edmonton?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is referring to the equalization issue. As I indicated in the House yesterday, these adjustments do not come as a surprise to any of the administrations because it is part and parcel of the formula which is legislated.
These adjustments are made at least two times a year. Sometimes the adjustments are upward and sometimes they are downward. In this particular case there are some provinces, particularly in the Atlantic region, that will experience a reduction. Nova Scotia, for example, will experience an increase while Manitoba and Saskatchewan will be favoured with an increase as a result of this adjustment process.
That is part of a legislated program, and I am sure the hon. member would not want us to tamper with that on an ad hoc basis.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's well camouflaged numbers do not deny the fact that a reduction in transfer dollars to the Northwest Territories means it is hopeless for northerners to have any economic security or even much needed infrastructure such as roads and airports.
In fact there is virtually no activity in the Beaufort Sea for oil and gas. There are crippling air costs because most of it is done by air travel. There are no mining incentives or tax deferral schemes.
October 23, 1991

My supplementary question to the minister would be: Will the minister undertake to ensure the newly elected Government of the Northwest Territories that his government will stop reducing opportunities for northerners by placing the burden of the federal deficit on the shoulders of northern Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while we have a serious fiscal problem, we certainly have not taken the issue of reducing the deficit solely on the backs of the provinces. For example, in 1984-84 transfers to the provinces totalled some $25.5 billion. In 1991-92 total transfers will equal $37 billion. That is a substantial increase.
In the area of equalization, in 1984-85 the transfers under equalization were $5.4 billion. This year it is $8.4 billion. EPF from $14.5 billion to $20,368 billion. The Canada Assistance Plan, in 1984-85 the transfers were $4 billion. In 1991-92 they are $6.3 billion.
It hardly suggests that there is a massive reduction in transfers to the provinces. I would interpret that as a massive increase in transfers to the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. It concerns Algoma as well.
The community action team is in Ottawa today representing a cross section of the communities of Sault Ste. Marie and Wawa. The minister is very aware of the facts surrounding this situation and he is also very aware of the requests we have made.
They are in the area of bridge pensions, older worker adjustment package, the necessary tax credits for employee buy-out and necessary funding for retraining.
It is the eleventh hour, and I ask the minister to provide specifics in which area the government will participate to give some reassurance to the delegation here today and to the communities of Sault Ste. Marie and Wawa.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Ttade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated, members of our government and of our caucus have met with the community action team.
They had extensive meetings yesterday and today with them. They discussed the range of issues that my hon. friend has read out. As I indicated in my previous answer, these are complex issues that involve a number of players and the discussions that are under way right now involve what is the appropriate sharing of the burden of meeting the challenges of this very complex situation.
Those discussions are continuing. My department, the Department of Employment and Immigration and other departments are fully engaged in these discussions. I think it would be premature for me to indicate with any precision because it is very difficult to do so at this stage of the discussions when we do not have the final answers from all the players around the table.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Labour.
The minister is aware of the present difficulties that the Canadian steel industry is facing. In Sault Ste. Marie and in Wawa, the situation is critical. Employees have already made many sacrifices in order to save their company and allow their communities to survive.
I want to ask the minister whether he is prepared to share some of the burden and whether the Older Workers Adjustment Program will be made more flexible for this company so that displaced older workers can be dealt with fairly.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member and commend him for his concern.
As far as the labour department is concerned, the lay-offs that have taken place are being studied by a committee of the province of Ontario and the federal government.
A report will be made to the Department of Labour and to me. At that time the decision will be made.

October 23, 1991
Oral Questions ATLANTIC ECONOMY

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
In September of this year, this cash starved federal government found hundreds of millions of dollars to spend in a doomed attempt to save two Tory premiers. Yet this week the Mulroney government stunned the Atlantic provinces with a cut of over $170 million in badly needed equalization payments.
Will the Minister of Finance stand up today and guarantee that federal funding to the Atlantic provinces will be maintained at a level sufficient to ensure that national standards can be maintained in the delivery of health care and social services by these four provincial governments, yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that it will be maintained consistent with the legislation and the formula that has been established.
I only remind the hon. member that equalization payments to the provinces have risen from $5.4 billion in 1984-85 to $8.4 billion in 1991-92. That is a substantial increase.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister.
Yesterday, the minister's press secretary said that "figures show the Atlantic economies are performing better than the other provinces".
Let us look at the facts. In Newfoundland, unemployment is 70 per cent above the national average. In Prince Edward Island, the per capita income is 32 per cent below the national average and in Nova Scotia, bankruptcies are at the highest rate in the country.
I ask the minister to stand and tell the tens of thousands of unemployed in the Atlantic region who are facing a winter on welfare, the students who cannot afford to pursue secondary education, or the sick waiting for hospital beds, whether he stands by these arrogant and objectionable statements made by his own department.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I don't want to deny
the fact that there are serious economic difficulties that all Canadians are facing, and I certainly appreciate the hon. member's concern about that, at the same time I think there has to be clear recognition of the fact that the federal government recognizes that there are poorer provinces, and in an effort to equalize opportunities and equalize services, we provide equalization grants.
Just for the record so that the hon. member will understand, for 1991-92 the equalization on a per capita basis to the province of Newfoundland is $1,649 per person; for Prince Edward Island it is $1,531 per person; for Nova Scotia it is $1,050 per person; and for New Brunswick it is $1,201 on a per capita basis.
As I indicated the level of equalization grants to the provinces has increased by 60 per cent since we have been in office.

Mr. Speaker, in the past year the federal government has cut transfer payments to Atlantic Canada by $164 million. The government speaks of competitiveness but it slashes post-secondary education funding. Dalhousie University, St. Mary's University, Mount St. Vincent University, to name three, have students, faculty and administrations that are bleeding from a thousand government inflicted wounds.
I ask the Minister of Finance today to tell us that he will restore established programs funding to its usual levels on a percentage basis, not just with his funny numbers game.

I repeat that total transfers to the provinces since we have come into office have increased from $25.6 billion to $37 billion in total transfers.
In terms of equalization, as I indicated earlier, the increase is from $5.4 billion to $8.4 billion, which is a 60 per cent increase.
It should be noted as well that today the Atlantic premiers in a press release said they decided not to ask Ottawa for more money to solve the financial crisis. They said they would concentrate on cutting costs and using
October 23, 1991

their resources more effectively. That is what we are all being asked to do.

A supplementary for the same minister, who now confirms that even the premiers down there have given up on him. He must know that that bafflegab doesn't pay university tuition fees and it does not shorten the wait for those who need elective surgery.
When is he going to beat some sense into his colleagues and call a halt now to this terrible pulverizing of health services, of post-secondary education, in Newfoundland and all across this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said in the House yesterday, you cannot have it both ways. The hon. member cannot have it both ways. All we are doing is applying the legislation that is there which enshrines the formula and enshrines the way in which these calculations are to be made.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
In the next few days the Canadian government will send a cabinet minister on a high level visit to China for the first time since the massacre at Tiananmen Square. conclusion. I think she knows she should not draw that conclusion.
We have taken a very sensitive view on exactly what is happening in China. The Minister of Agriculture is visiting there on a mission to see whether there are ways that we can promote agricultural exports to China, China being one of our largest customers over many, many years. We have indicated consistently since Tiananmen Square our concern about human rights problems within China. We have made it very clear that as we have changed our approach marginally during this period to allow certain types of exchanges, that should not be interpreted in any way as condoning any of the human rights abuses that have occurred in China.

I have a supplementary question for the same minister, Mr. Speaker. I have just returned from China. I raised specific issues on human rights violations with top level Chinese officials. We know the situation is still appalling and yet they skirted my questions.

I say to the Liberal Party that you cannot have it both ways. On the one side it is saying: "We must do more for the farmers. We must provide a greater degree of support to the farmers" and then on the other hand: "We can't support agricultural trade with China". You cannot have it both ways.

Mr. Speaker, I have had discussions with the parliamentary secretary to the House leader opposite. I seek consent from the House to express condolences on behalf of all members of Parliament to the Herman Batten family.
Herman Batten was a member of Parliament from 1953 to 1968 and passed away last night at the age of 82. Herman Batten was my predecessor in the riding of Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte. In fact his constituency at one point, as other members who have been here longer than I will recall, included all of western, northwestern and southwestern Newfoundland.
He was re-elected six times and served as Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons. He will be remembered as the gentleman who was the chairman of the House of Commons flag committee and sought to maintain a modicum of order in what was a very emotional and divisive debate. Perhaps it reminds us somewhat of the debate that goes on in this countiy today. But he was able, through great patience, great sensitivity and great understanding to find consensus and
October 23, 1991

to produce, as chairman of the flag committee, a new flag for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, he was a member of Parliament when you could not fly back to Ottawa in a couple of hours. He was a member of Parliament when you had to visit most of rural Newfoundland by boat. He was one who was held near and dear by his constituents. He served with great distinction and great compassion. He shall be remembered in the Liberal Party. He shall be remembered I know in this Parliament and, in particular, he will be remembered with a great deal of warmth and fondness by the people of western Newfoundland.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you and my colleagues for this opportunity to express our appreciation for Herman Batten and our condolences to his family.

speechtext:

I want to draw particular attention to his work as a committee chairman. That is a role that we in this House give a great deal of dignity and I, being a boy scout back in 1968, can remember some of the emotion that was generated with that particular debate.
Having served as a chairman in this House, I know that when you have a controversial issue, it is a great test of character to be able to go through an issue that is so difficult and so divisive and yet has to be addressed in terms of what is good for the country.
I want to conclude once again by saying that on behalf of members on this side of the House, we express to the family of Mr. Herman Batten and to his friends our sincere sorrow to hear of his passing.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party I want to say how saddened we were when we heard of the passing of
Tribute
Herman Batten and our condolences go out to his family and his friends.
As others have indicated, he was known as a constituency man. He served the constituency well. He was a friend of everyone in the constituency. If my memory serves me, he was re-elected six times as a show of good faith by his constituents in the work he did on their behalf.
Also, those who knew him and those who read Hansard know of the role that he played in some very critical debates in the House of Commons. He was a man who was not afraid to speak up for his constituents and was not hesitant at all to speak on the critical issues of the day.
When we heard of the news of his passing we were very saddened and our thoughts and our condolences go out to his friends and his family.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to rise and say a word on the passing of Mr. Herman Batten, the former member for the old riding of Humber-St. George's, a good chunk of which is now part of the riding of Burin-St. George's which I have the honour to represent here.
In so doing, I pay tribute to a great Canadian, to a compassionate Newfoundlander and to an absolutely marvellous human being. He is remembered fondly and often by his constituents, indeed his name came up in a conversation just a few days ago in my riding.
As Deputy Speaker of this House he represented the institution with great dignity and great purpose and we salute him for that. He will be remembered by those who heard him speak from this Chamber and elsewhere for he had a very rich baritone voice and a very impressive intellect to match.
His family and his friends, who are legion, can be consoled in the sure knowledge that he lived a good, full life and touched the lives of many for the better because of his great integrity and compassion.

Madam Speaker, as one who knew Herman Batten personally in this House, I would like to say a word about him today.
In Newfoundland he was known as a schoolmaster. He sat in the chair of this House and brought great dignity to

October 23, 1991

that position. He had that great, deep voice that automatically communicated the fact that he meant business.
Whenever you met him on the street you would see him wearing the good old black hat that was so prominent in those days and in previous days. He looked like an educator. He was a professional person in every way. He had the ability to handle very difficult problems with ease because he was cool, he had a candour and one could tell that he dealt with many problems before coming to this House and he handled them here extremely well.
I remember Herman Batten as a fine gentleman, a very effective parliamentarian, a man with coolness and dignity in this Chamber. He was missed very much after he left here because he did do such a great job in the Chair.
I would like to take this opportunity to extend our condolences to his family, and to say to his constituents who knew him so well in those days that they had great wisdom in selecting him as their member of the House of Commons of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I rise on the same point of privilege and do so with a little trepidation. I am glad the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke spoke because he and I were here when the Hon. Mr. Batten was here and was Deputy Speaker. I cast no reflection on the fine comments made about Mr. Batten the individual.
Madam Speaker, I really do think that in this House of Commons we have to start to get criteria about the eulogies to members who have come, and other distinguished Canadians who have passed away, having served Canada.
Monday, for instance, we had freelanced here on a point of privilege the death of an outstanding Canadian, 91 years old, a Mr. Nicholson. He used to be a member of this House of Commons. I almost rose then, as I should have done, because in my experience here for a few years I have never heard so many tributes. We have become the house of eulogies rather than the House of Commons. I have written a letter to the Speaker. This is no reflection at all on all those we referred to, but when I hear some of the words, Madam Speaker, about how they are all sorely missed, after 10, 15, 20 or 30 years I really question how members can say that who never were here when the member we are talking about served in this House. It thus discounts and dilutes the tributes that have to be made on those occasions that used to be
reserved for this period. But it should not be for every former comrade who has fallen by the wayside because of the natural reflection of time.
I really hope the Speaker takes this under consideration and can give some criteria to House leaders so that we all know. We did something the other day that I do not remember having done before. I may be out of tune, but certainly, Mr. Blackburn, when you go we will try to remember you.
Who was it the other day?

We had the Supreme Court Justice, Madam Speaker, a very fine Canadian. But now do we do it for every Federal Court judge? Do we do it for the Chief Justice of the provinces?
I think there are many little matters in this regard. Instead of diluting the tributes that used to be on the floor of the House, we should have criteria to make them worth while for those we try to remember in the best way.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present the first report of the Standing Committee on Environment pertaining to the Porcupine caribou herd calving grounds in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in the state of Alaska.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present to the House a petition signed by residents in Jasper and other communities in Alberta and British Columbia urging the Department of the Environment to keep the Jasper airstrip open.

Madam Speaker, it is an honour for me to present a petition on behalf of probably more than 100 residents of Edmonton with respect to a great woman, Marie Sklodowska Curie, that she might be honoured for her scientific contributions to humanity. The signers of the petition believe
that the gift of the discovery of radium to heal the sick of the world deserves to be recognized in our country.
The petitioners call on Canada Post to honour Madam Curie by the issuing of a commemorative stamp on the occasion of the 125th anniversary of her birth on November 7, 1992. It is my pleasure to tender the petition.

Madam Speaker, I have two petitions. The first one is from residents of Val-d'Or, Joutel, Vassan, Quebec City, Montreal North, Sainte-Catherine and Saint-Emond, who respectfully submit to Parliament that the Canada Labour Code must respect the principle set forth in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and is therefore supposed to protect the rights of women; and that preventive withdrawal for pregnant women is a desirable and necessary option for women in the workplace. They call upon Parliament to recognize the need for including clauses in the Code concerning preventive withdrawal of pregnant women, with pay.

Madam Speaker, my second petition concerns firearms. It is from a group of petitioners who are residents of Ottawa, Gatineau and Gloucester. Whereas access to firearms is a critical factor in homicide, accidents and suicide; and whereas in Canada many kinds of weapons are readily available which are not needed for legitimate purposes such as hunting or competitive shooting, your petitioners ask Parliament to adopt legislation that will prohibit the possession of firearms by any person with a criminal record.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to present a petition on behalf of a number of residents of Barriere, Louis Creek, Kamloops and Darfield, British Columbia. They are concerned about a proposal to divert the North Thompson River at Valemount into the Columbia River channel, which will eventually move water from British Columbia to the San Diego, California area. That is part of the plan.

They are simply asking the Government of Canada to ensure that proper funding is kept in place to ensure proper RCMP police protection.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That this House recognize that it is the national forum for the consideration of issues and challenges facing all Canadians;
That this House recognizes that its Members were elected by the people of Canada to represent them in a manner which demands that individual Members respect one another and their democratic right to express differing opinions;
That Canadians have expressed alarm at the excessive partisanship and lack of decorum and civility too often in evidence in the House;
That this House recognize that disruptive behaviour and verbal interruptions, including abusive language, leads to a depreciated view of and respect for the institution of Parliament and its Members;
That the Members of this House share in the responsibility of eliminating the use of offensive language or gestures directed at other Members either during Question Period, debate or otherwise in the Chamber; and
That this House supports the Speaker's vigorous enforcement of Standing Order 16(2) and Standing Order 18; in particular those portions which require that when a Member is speaking no Member shall interrupt him or her except to raise a point of order and that no Member shall speak disrespectfully or use offensive words against either House or any Member thereof.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion today had its genesis some months ago when the whole concern about the operation of the House, its effectiveness, efficiency and reputation became a matter of some public debate.
I have spoken on this issue for many months in the context of House reform and in seeking ways to improve the institution, make it more responsive and restore faith in it.
We had independent confirmation of the disrepute in which we were held in the Spicer report. It is interesting to recall that the Spicer report was a result of the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future. The issue before the forum was one of constitutional reform, one of the unity of this country. In pursuing its mandate the commission held public hearings literally everywhere in the country to ask people about their concerns about this

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
country. With a rather disturbing frequency people raised the question of Parliament and how it carries on.
I would like to quote an anecdote from a group in Ontario on page 97 of the Spicer report: "Just terrible the way they carry on in Parliament, like unruly children, bad tempered brats, no control, quarrelling between parties. Why don't they get together and use their better ideas". As I said, this was not an isolated anecdote incident and it was repeated in many parts of the country by many groups. In the report's conclusions, the commission states on page 136 of the report: "We join with forum participants in deploring the mindless, and sometimes disgraceful, behaviour of members of both Houses in bringing the parliamentary system into disrepute. We agree with the forum's participants who have pointed out constantly to the fact that our system is too partisan and far too adversarial. In particular, we would urge a careful review of Question Period and how it is organized with an eye on the more productive Question Periods in other parliamentary systems".
If we are to fulfil our responsibilities as members of Parliament, we have to take that observation and those recommendations seriously. We must act to change that view of ourselves and this Chamber. Canadians from coast to coast are identifying this Chamber and our behaviour in it as part of the fundamental constitutional problems of this country.
Let us make it clear that this is not in itself an adversarial debate. I do not intend to engage in finger pointing and I am prepared to admit that I am as adversarial as others in this House. I am sure that other parties have gone through the record as I have. I am sure there are quotes the House leader of the Liberal Party would not like to be reminded of. I have some quotes that the House leader of the New Democratic Party would not like to be reminded of, and I am sure there are quotes that I would rather not be reminded of.
Books.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I understand that. However, that does not change our responsibility as members of Parliament to address the concern which Canadians have stressed from coast to coast.
Some have suggested that the introduction of television in this House is the root of the problem. There is
some merit to that suggestion. Television is first and foremost an entertainment media. Television finds conflict, theatrics, fighting, and the adversarial aspects of politics irresistible. That is not a conspiracy. Television reporters are not somehow bad. It is simply a fact of life. Television brings this institution into the living rooms of virtually every home in this country. Television is here to stay; the technology is here to stay. We have to recognize that and conduct ourselves accordingly.
I think the media can help by understanding that and understanding their responsibility. I am reminded of two incidents which I think make the point. In one instance a member of this House stood up and made the accusation that a member opposite was lying. The Speaker quite properly asked that the remark be withdrawn and the member did. However that night the clip of the member standing up theatrically declaring somebody opposite a liar was used on television.
A member of my staff telephoned the producer of that program and said that this was rather unfair since withdrawal was tantamount to it not being said. Television is supposed to be electronic Hansard and by running something that was withdrawn it in essence gave a false impression of what was happening here. That type of occurrence tends to create that type of activity because we are all human and are in politics because we desire and need to be exposed to the public. If television is going to cover antics such as breaking the rules then the temptation to do that is overwhelming.
In fairness, I must say that CTV examined the tape, examined what happened and said it agreed that it should not have done that. It is now CTV's policy that it will not run clips of statements that have been withdrawn.
Just the other day in the House a member said "hypocrite", a word that is not to be used in this House, and he withdrew it. However some of the print media ran that line. It was withdrawn, it was supposed not to have been said, but it was run.
We also telephoned that particular institution and drew its attention to what it was doing when it treated what our rules say is invalid in here as valid criticism. The institution had encouraged it and it should not be done. In that case we did not get a commitment to change
October 23, 1991

policy but we did get an acknowledgement that there was a problem which needed to be addressed.
I repeat again that I do not suggest this is partisan, that one side is more sinful or sinless than the other. We are all partisans in an institution which we all respect. However sometimes in our partisan zeal we behave in ways which bring this institution into disrespect.
We have been speaking about the need for change for better behaviour, but I do not think we have demonstrated that desire through our behaviour and our words. We talk about the need to change but have not really demonstrated it as a body. There are rules in existence guiding decorum and offensive language, and I think it is time and appropriate to reassert the commitment of members of this House to these fundamental rules.
For instance, Standing Order 16(2) states specifically that when a member is speaking no member shall interrupt him or her except to raise a point of order. That Standing Order is honoured in the breach more than it is in practice. I venture to say it would be difficult to find a day in which someone on their feet, either asking a question or answering one in Question Period, is not being shouted at, heckled, and barracked from the opposite benches. That is contrary to the Standing Orders of this House.
If we do not believe those Standing Orders should be there perhaps we should take them out. However, I think we believe they should be there. Perhaps we should be asking ourselves to follow the Standing Orders and ask that they be enforced if we too often behave more like members of a mob than individual responsible members of Parliament.
Standing Order 18 says that no member shall speak disrespectfully or use offensive words against any other member. Of course we all know that is violated virtually every day in this institution, mainly in Question Period, but in debate as well.
They are pretty clear. We do not follow them. Maybe we should. The public out there is demanding that we do. Those are the Standing Orders. Beauchesne's, our procedural bible so to speak which lays out how we should engage in debate in Question Period, is again violated virtually on a daily basis. A rule respecting Oral Questions, citation 409, paragraph 7 of Beauchesne's sixth edition, says:
Government Orders
A question must adhere to the proprieties of the House, in terms
of inferences, imputing motives or casting aspersions upon persons
within the House or out of it.
In other words, we should not impute motives or cast aspersions upon persons in this House. We do it all the time. Lest that just refer to the questioner, it says in terms of reply to Oral Questions, page 120, citation 408, paragraph 2.
Answers to questions should be as brief as possible, should deal
with the matter raised and should not provoke debate.
I hesitate to say that a lot of the answers provoke heckling, barracking and debate. And that is true as well.
Maybe we should ask ourselves if Beauchesne is obsolete and from a day gone by. Perhaps nowadays it is appropriate to heckle, barrack, provoke debate, impute motives and do all of those things that precedents in this book say are inappropriate.
If they are still appropriate today, let us agree and collectively do what we can to condition ourselves. We must ask our presiding officer to bring us back into control when our emotions or better judgment gets out of control. It is something we should seriously ask.
Shouting across the floor, barracking and constantly interrupting members is not necessary. It does not aid understanding. It does not improve the quality of life of Canadians and it is contrary to the rules. If we obeyed the rules a greater calm would prevail, the atmosphere would be more conducive to speaking and listening to responsible and fair debate.
We do not need to shout, yell and barrack insults in order to carry out our responsibilities to govern the country, to be held accountable and to raise issues of concern to our constituents. This is what this debate is all about. Name calling or slurs are not appropriate and neither are they acceptable. Theatrical outbursts and actions denigrate this Chamber and, by extension, the people we are here to represent.
Like storming the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am trying to keep this on the high road. The member for Halifax, speaking from her seat, talks about storming the chair.

I knew you did not do it, Harvie.

October 23, 1991

speechtext: The member for Kingston and the Islands will be able to tell his colleague that he saw the clip and knows that did not occur. There is continuous repetition of that slur. She is not the only one, I can assure you, who has used that over the years.

Mr. Andre And there is the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood interrupting me from his seat as well. It is that sort of-
You are casting aspersions on her.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the interjections opposite probably make my point better than I could.
You are a phoney.
Will the hon. member withdraw. The hon. member is completely out of order. I would ask that he withdraw "you are a phoney", please.
I humbly withdraw my remarks. The cheap shots-

I do not want a further argument about it. It was very clear and I have no other course than to ask the hon. member to withdraw. The hon. member has withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps it is not possible for us to put our partisanship aside, but I think we need to try. I again commend those of us in here who worry about these things to read some of the things that are said about this institution in the citizen's forum.
The government.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The House leader from the New Democratic Party is interrupting me.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. In light of the comments made by my hon. friend and colleague, surely while we are listening to his interesting comments we are allowed to muse aloud.
There is no intention to heckle. There is no intention to interrupt. It is just that when I hear some of his comments, for example when he referred to the Spicer commission's reports and commentary on behaviour
here, I was simply musing aloud. The Spicer commission had a lot to say about the Prime Minister as well.
I am not interrupting him. I am not causing difficulty. I am just musing aloud.
Surely to goodness we do not have to sit here in mute silence for every second of the day while we listen to someone like the government House leader speak.
If you are asking my opinion you are treading into dangerous ground indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose we should put in here, then, musing aloud is allowed. I do not know.
Seriously I have been here for 19 years and I know some would say that is too long. I will anticipate the remarks on the other side. It becomes less and less of an honour to describe one's occupation as a member of Parliament, given the kinds of comments that one reads and hears about in terms of this institution.
Again I am not finger pointing in terms of the problems being over there as opposed to over here or any such thing. I am simply making an observation which I believe behoves us all to recognize that the public does not hold this institution in great esteem.
I think it is time that we recognize that. I think it would be appropriate for the House collectively, for all of us on all sides, to say: "Yes, there is a problem here".
We can for our partisan advantages say who is more the problem than the other side and so on and so forth. If we choose to do that, perhaps we can do that outside. Perhaps we can do that by way of a press release or out in the scrums. In here we can treat each other with respect and with the commitment that we believe equally that whatever our differences and views we are sincere in our views and we are here because we want to serve this country.
We are not here for the purpose of demeaning those whose views are different from ours or those on opposite sides of the House. It is the service of the country that motivates us all. We must recognize that we need to address the reputation of this institution.
We ask our presiding officer to recognize that we are weak. We fail. We let our emotions get out of hand and we call on him to be superior to the rest of us; not let his emotions get out of hand but to keep us under control and identify us publicly when we misbehave. That is a pretty significant penalty for the folks back home to see
October 23, 1991

the Speaker identify the member for Calgary Centre or say the government House leader should not speak from his seat if he is not recognized. That is a significant penalty. But the Speaker cannot do it if we do not agree to it.
I am asking colleagues in this House to agree that we have a problem, that we are going to address it collectively, and that we are going to try to restore the reputation of this institution and make Canadians proud of us rather than embarrassed about us.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order to designate tomorrow as an allotted day.
The House resumed consideration of motion of Mr. Andre (p. 3871).

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this afternoon to participate in this debate. I want to say a few things about how we got here today, for the record, so that Mr. Speaker will be fully aware of what has gone on and who has been informed about the substance of this particular motion.
I want to say to the government House leader that he is accurate in his intervention in that the subject matter itself has been discussed among House leaders, but certainly the motion itself has not been a subject matter for House leaders. This has been placed on the Order Paper and, I might underline, it is the right of the government House leader to do so.
Having said that, I have listened attentively to what the minister has said. I wish to quote the second paragraph of the motion. It states:
That this House recognizes that its Members were elected by the people of Canada to represent them in a manner which demands that individual Members respect one another and their democratic right to express differing opinions.
Government Orders
How true that is, but the House leader opposite goes on to quote as his authority the comments and the conclusions of the Spicer commission. I want to be careful here because I do not want to misquote him. I think he said "independent confirmation of the disrepute of parliamentarians" and the citation that he used was Mr. Spicer and the commission which travelled the country.
I know that the hon. member opposite selected a few pages which had references with regard to Question Period. I want to quote for the hon. member opposite some of the words of a friend of mine, of members of the New Democratic Party, of that side, and perhaps even a dear friend of the Minister of Employment and Immigration at one time. He is one of the commissioners who was appointed by the Prime Minister to the Spicer commission, Richard Cashin. Here is what he said. I think this is worth noting. As many members know, he was a former member of this House and served with some degree of distinction in the deliberations of this House.
I am quoting from page 141 of that text. It states:
From the outset there were those who expressed the hope that this process would do more than just solicit the views of Canadians. Unfortunately for a variety of reasons we were unable, as some commissioners would have liked, to deepen the dialogue.
He goes on:
Public opinion must be respected for its complexity and we must recognize that people's views on subjects change with the information they have and the thoroughness of the debate.
He further states:
The people who spoke to us expressed opinion on many matters. We have no way of knowing how their opinions on one matter were related to their opinions on other matters or what priority particular issues may have had in their thinking. Nor do we have any way of knowing how representative the opinions we hear may be of the opinions of all Canadians. This is because the process of participation was self-selective.
And I underline that. I put that on the record not to challenge the government House leader but to balance the views. The view that he is putting forward as I understand it-and I stand to be corrected-is that the operation of this House, and in particular Question Period, is despicable and is held in much disregard by Canadians. That is one view.
There is another view of a commissioner on the Spicer commission who says that the views which were put forward to the Spicer commission on many occasions were not challenged. There was no thoroughness of debate. There was no comprehensive dialogue going on

Government Orders
between those participants and those that were making the presentations.
I would ask, did the Spicer commission make a distinction between opposition MPs asking questions and ministers responding to those questions? I have read the Spicer commission report and I did not see any distinction on that.
Is it possible, I ask the Chair, that Canadians who have watched our deliberations may not like the length of the hon. member's hair, may not like the way the hon. member poses his question, may not like the way the hon. member phrases a couple of words? Or could it be possible that Canadians are not very happy with the responses on free trade? They may not be happy with the responses they have received on the GST, or the vagueness of the answer, or on Constitutional matters, regional development, CBC cutbacks, or proliferation of taxes. Make no mistake about it, Canadians out there today are angry. They are angry at Parliament, at provincial institutions, because the economy of this country is in such bad shape that they want their legislators in Ottawa to take concrete, positive action and to date they have not seen that. They have not seen that in the last number of months.
Absolutely. Right on.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think that must be said. My colleague makes reference to the TV networks. I think this is a point I share with the hon. member opposite. If there is a withdrawal made by an hon. member, it would be inappropriate for TV networks to carry the exact intervention without having the withdrawal stated as well.
The hon. member talks about breaches of certain Standing Orders of the House of Commons. Implicit in his argument, and I am not suggesting he has said this, is that there have been numerous breaches of the Standing Orders. I disagree. I think there have been breaches of the Standing Orders, there is no question. In a Chamber of 300 persons or so, yes, you are going to get breaches of the Standing Orders. But I have full confidence that the Chair is our arbitrator, is impartial and will draw to the attention of members in the House when those rules have been broken. I think all hon. members on all sides of the House would want to concur with that.
The government House leader has said that this Chamber is quite a theatre and that from time to time people may use language or expressions which may make the front pages of newspapers or clips on television. I have to tell the hon. member, and I say this to you, Mr. Speaker, because not only are we debating the pith and substance of the motion before us, we are also debating the spirit of the motion.
It has to be said that when I was elected to represent my constituents, with youth unemployment in excess of 17 per cent, adult unemployment in excess of 25 per cent and upwards to 40 per cent in parts of my constituency- and I see other members here who have similar concerns on all sides of this House-I was not asked to come to Parliament to stand in my place and say to the Prime Minister: Mr. Prime Minister, you are such a wonderful person, what are you going to do for Canada today?
I was not elected to do that. I am sorry. People have difficulty with that and I think the people that have the greatest difficulty with that are members on the government benches.
I say that with great sincerity. If we transcend the boundaries of proper wording, conduct and behaviour, it is obviously left to the Chair to bring us back to order. However, let us not portray ourselves as individuals who come here, stand in our place with hand on heart and say in monotone voice: "Well, you know, what can you do for Canada today? That is just not the way it is. Each member is different".
Many members on our side of the House have great fluency in the English language. That is something I do not have. A number of members have great fluency in the French language. That is something I do not have. However, I am duly elected and am a representative of my people, as all of these members are. Mr. Speaker, as the arbitrator in this great Chamber, you must acknowledge that as a fact of life of the process of democracy and representative government.
The motion before us today is in response to certain recent happenings in this House. I have been a member of this House for well over 10 years and have seen previous occasions where tempers have flared, behaviour was unbecoming, words were exchanged, withdrawals
October 23, 1991

took place, et cetera. However, to suggest and imply that rules are being continuously broken every day, that no co-operation exists between opposition parties and that the government on various pieces of legislation is just not true.
Perhaps myself and the parliamentary secretary should be holding press conferences along with the House leader of New Democratic Party to tell them how we have co-operated on different measures. If you were listening to members opposite you would think that we co-operate on nothing, and that is not true. Mr. Speaker, you must know that and understand that notwithstanding the comments which may have been written in different newspapers and made by different individuals there is a fair amount of co-operation.
We as a party are not opposed to the thrust of this motion. There is a line of acceptable behaviour and in recent weeks it has been crossed by two government backbenchers, and there have been other incidents involving members from all political parties. We believe that we have to do something about it before the problem grows.
In light of these events in this Chamber we have to send a message to our electors that we are aware of the need for ameliorating our conduct and that we will act on it. No one disputes that we are expected to behave in a civil manner. Indeed our constituents expect it of us. However, they simultaneously expect us to defend their interest with passion and conviction.
If the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood comes into this House as a new member and stands on the floor of this House of Commons to make a case for a refugee or a small business person or an individual who is unemployed and does it with conviction, as he normally does, and with great flamboyance, so be it. No Speaker of this House should deny that member that particular right and no governing party should try to restrict a member in the expression of his or her views on that subject matter.
We would be remiss in our duty if we did not relay the fact that what goes on in this House is adversarial. It is an adversarial process. This is not a high school debate; it is an adversarial process. That is what we were sent here
Government Orders
for, and we in the opposition are expected to do our best in holding the government accountable.
I know the government House leader agrees with me on this because he made this very point on June 13,1980, and I quote from Hansard at page 2082:
Given the nature of this Chamber where we face each other two sword lengths apart, if members shout order at us we will respond in kind. We will shout order back. If they refuse to answer questions or if they abuse the Question Period you can expect that we will respond in kind. That would be only natural. If we were to do anything else we would be failing in our responsibility as an opposition to keep the government in check.
The government House leader was politically correct in 1980, and I suggest that stands today on October 23,
1991.	Although we have profound differences and struggle with each other in debate daily we should not cross the threshold to personal attacks. That is counterproductive to the work of this place. That is what makes Canadians unhappy and cynical with their elected officials.
That being said, we on this side of the House have a few questions and worries pertaining to the motion itself. The government wants the House to limit excessive partisanship. The question that then arises is: Who will define excessive partisanship? If the Chair is expected to it could result in the immediate loss of confidence in the Chair. The Chair would be in fact choosing a side or, as they say on the street, lining up with one of the parties.
I cannot stress enough the importance of the independence of the Chair. When a member of this Chamber wears the black robe of impartiality he or she is the only member of this House whose non-partisanship is required. The call on partisanship is not to be left to the Chair. As I have said that would leave the Chair open to accusations of partisanship itself.
I am concerned by another omission in this motion. That is the explicit wording of the deplored use of sexist and racial language. That is not only beyond the realm of heated debate turned personal but is the realm of uncivilized barbarism. The politics of hate is an enemy of this Chamber and all humanity and must be confronted and stopped.
Just because we are in this House does not make us immune to those traits of society which are unacceptable. First, we have to mend our own ways. Second, if we do cross that line between intense political struggle and

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
abusive behaviour I have complete confidence, as does my party, in the Chair's ability to enforce the rules of this Chamber accordingly.
Despite what the government House leader thought in 1980, he often complains of raw partisanship on the floor of the House. I for one prefer to be shooting words across the floor than bullets across a square. I would rather be wrestling in inflammatory debate than be beaten to the ground by a billy stick. I would rather be face to face in this Chamber with hon. members opposite than face to face with a tank.
No one said that democracy was easy. However, the struggles here in this House are infinitely preferable to the alternatives. We have a great institution in this country, many say a model for modem democracies. Canadians should be proud of their political traditions. We have to work to clean up our act so that we never have to contemplate those alternatives.
The system may not always work to perfection and it may not present a pretty picture, but as Sir Winston Churchill once observed: "Democracy is the worst form of government except all of the others".
In conclusion, we as a party support the basic thrust of this motion. We believe sexism and racism should be specified. We believe our confidence in the ability of the present Speaker should be clearly expressed. I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the word "offensive" and by substituting the following therefor:
-including sexist or racist language or gestures directed at other members, either during Question Period, debate or otherwise in the Chamber; and
That this House confirms its support for Standing Orders 16 and 18, and other Standing Orders and practices of this House regarding decorum and reaffirms its confidence in the Speaker's ability to enforce those rules and practices vigorously.
