Continuing debate, the hon. member for Kamloops.
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to say at the outset as the amendment indicates that we too have full faith in the ability of the Speaker to manage the affairs of this House appropriately-
Hear, hear.

We want to congratulate you on your excellent work, Mr. Speaker.
I want to begin my remarks by saying that I have listened carefully to the government House leader's comments and certainly do not question his motive. I believe that his intentions regarding this motion were indeed honourable and that he means well.
I must say that he has absolutely and totally missed the boat. If the government House leader really believes that changing a rule or two in the House of Commons is somehow going to transform this place into a corporate board room where everything is done very businesslike and with a very clear agenda with little partisan debate, he is dreaming in Technicolor.
Can you imagine politics in the House of Commons?
Talk about dull.

We have partisanship in the House of Commons. The House is set up with the government on the right-hand side of the Speaker and the opposition parties on the left-hand side of the Speaker. It is set up in such a way that it is a confrontational situation. It is little wonder that the debate in here is often very aggressive and very focused on critical comments directed at the government. So it should be.
With all due respect, and without questioning the motive behind this motion, I think the government House leader simply has failed to understand what it is that frustrates Canadians about this place.
I must say that from time to time the behaviour could be improved. Sometimes the antics can be inappropriate. It is with some sadness and regret in my heart that I recall incidences in the last few days of racist and sexist remarks and rude and crude gestures made by certain members on a certain side of the House, which we were all disgusted with. We found them to be completely inappropriate and were disappointed that no action was taken by the respective leaders of the parties. I was very proud of the fact that when this was taking place our leader made it very clear that she felt that it was a responsibility of the leadership in the caucus whether it is the leader, the House leader, or the Whip to ensure that the appropriate behaviour takes place. When that appropriate behaviour is transgressed and members are found to be behaving inappropriately action must be taken.

It is clear what action should be taken. People can be removed of their positions and others. It was a sad day in this House when some of the rudest comments made by members were passed over in a rather casual way by the leadership of the caucus.
I think we missed an opportunity at that point to ensure that we take this place seriously and do not condone that type of behaviour. Unfortunately it was a missed opportunity.
There is no question that there is an element of frustration in this House from time to time and it is reflected in the country. My hon. colleague quoted from the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future or the Spicer commission, and I noticed that his comments were very selective.
I want to ask the government House leader to turn to page 131 where it says:
As a result many participants felt betrayed and bereft and are confused and angry. Part of this is due to their sense that traditional Canadian values are being usurped by anonymous market forces and that governments are doing nothing to deal with these. Governments are in part responsible for these fears which we believe come from misunderstandings that governments must clarify or continue to pay a heavy price for as will our country.
In other words what the people of Canada are saying is that this place is not responsive to their needs. When we found ourselves involved in a crisis such as the Desert Storm situation, there was no debate in the House of Commons reflecting the people of Canada as to the appropriate role that Canada should play. That was presumably made in secret by some group.
When the Oka crisis was upon us was there a debate in the House as the appropriate course of action? No. Again decisions were made on behalf of the country in secret. When it was decided to cut back on critical passenger rail service was there a debate in the House of Commons on the appropriateness of these measures? No. It was done in secret by the government.
I could go on and on identifying item after item why people of Canada have felt frustrated, why people of Canada have felt that this Parliament of theirs is irrelevant. There is not a better example than the goods and services tax. Here was a tax that was going to touch the
Government Orders
lives of every single Canadian from small children to elderly citizens virtually every day of their lives.
When other governments imposed taxes, they took action when they heard from the people of the country in terms of their concern and their outrage. They responded with some sensitivity.
The United Kingdom in its wisdom at one time decided to impose a poll tax. The reaction was what one would predict. It was an extremely heavy reaction against that initiative. The government listened and the House of Commons and the House of Lords debated the issue and the government decided to back off from that tax. It listened to the people.
In Japan they imposed their version of the goods and services tax. There was a strong outcry and they said it was a wrong move and they backed off in part from this goods and services tax.
Have we heard a shred of sensitivity from the government in terms of what this GST is doing to our country and to the people of Canada? Unfortunately no.
I suspect that is why the people of Canada are so frustrated. That is why they say their politicians have betrayed them. What they mean is that the Government of Canada has betrayed them, the members of the government have betrayed them.
We have seen in recent days, indeed in recent weeks, that when people have been given the opportunity to show what they think of their governments they have changed their governments dramatically. In Ontario, British Columbia and Saskatchewan, to give you the most recent examples, they changed those governments when they had an opportunity because they felt they had been unreceptive.
I do not think the government House leader understands the problem if he thinks that by enforcing a couple of Standing Orders it will somehow magically change this place. Again I say I do not question his motives, but I do not think he understands the problem.
The problem has been the inability of this government to respond to the needs of the people of Canada. It has imposed upon them a corporate agenda that they find alien and reject, yet the government shows no sensitivity to the errors of its ways.

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
Another reason for the frustration in this House is the unprecedented use of closure or various forms of closure. The government has imposed forms of closure to muzzle members of Parliament and closed down debates at every stage of some bills, the GST and the free trade agreement being the most obvious.
In the annotated Standing Orders on page 22 they provide members of Parliament with a little history about the use of closure or the limiting of debate on issues. They say that one occurred in 1913 over the naval bill. Nothing much happened until 1956 during the pipeline debate. Again closure was used, but we have now seen closure as a regular event. Introduce a bill and, if it takes more than a day or two at a certain reading, the government just gives notice of closure. It has changed the Standing Orders to make it even easier and debate is then brought to an end. No wonder members of Parliament feel frustrated and at times perhaps lose their tempers.
I would now like to mention the committee system. Committees with the odd exception are almost a waste of time. Members of Parliament often work very hard, and time and time again the government simply ignores their recommendations and all the work that has been put into those committee meetings.
I want to say that if there is a behavioural problem in this House we have to accept responsibility. We do not have to blame you, Mr. Speaker, and that is what this motion does. This motion is sort of a subtle way of storming the chair. Granted we are not up there as we were-and I remember that day vividly-sitting right back there, Mr. Speaker. I remember the day and it was one of the saddest days of my life. Members roared up to the chair, banging and shaking their fists in the Speaker's face. I remember that day.
This in a way is another form of that. This motion says that you are not doing your job properly. I say that we do not accept that. We do not accept that.
If we are looking to place responsibility, whether it is an organization, a club, a firm or a business, the person at the helm sets a certain tone. If you have a good club, Mr. Speaker, you probably have a good club president; if you have a very effective firm, you probably have a good president of that firm; if you have some organization that is really doing its job well and accomplishing a great deal,
it is likely because of the certain tone that president or that chairperson sets.
Who is it that sets the tone in this House? It is the Prime Minister. It is the Prime Minister. It is the government House leader. He sets the tone. He is the one during Question Period who decides whether to respond to questions or not, and therein lies a great deal of frustration.
Yesterday during Question Period a member referred to the news media saying that our Prime Minister was being considered for Secretary-General of the United Nations. In good faith the question was put to him: "Have you agreed to let your name stand for that position?" Did he respond then to a serious question, a question that was on the minds presumably of every Canadian? No. He skated around the issue, a little bit of theatrics, a little bit of fun back and forth with the Leader of the Opposition about how hopeful he was for an election coming up, and so on.
People watching that exchange would be frustrated and would ask: "Why doesn't the Prime Minister answer the question?" There is an element of frustration out there that is unbelievable against our Prime Minister. Going back to the Spicer report, the government House leader did not read it all or at least he did not quote it all. The last page of the Spicer report, page 168, concludes with the views of Canadians on the Prime Minister's leadership. Virtually 100 per cent of the letters and the phone calls were negative toward him. The graph on this page is almost unbelievable. One hundred per cent of the respondents had little or no faith in the Prime Minister. Therein lies one of the reasons for the frustration felt across the country and in this House because we are the people who represent that frustration.
My friend, the government House leader, says we should all behave here like gentlemen and indeed we do mostly.
Excuse me.
Gentlepersons.
Excuse me.

Gentlepeople. When I go back to Kamloops and talk to my constituents they say: "Nelson, go down to the House of Commons" and I cannot repeat what they suggest I should do. They are not suggesting that I simply stand up here and act in a very quiet way, trying to be positive and compliment the government on all of its

great initiatives and adding calmly to some suggestions. Oh, yes, they probably expect me to do that from time to time, but they suggest what I should do when I get down here and confront this Prime Minister and what I should do when I get into the House of Commons to raise issues of concern to the people of Kamloops. I could not do 98 per cent of the things they want me to do. That is how strongly they feel, how frustrated and how angry they feel, and it is reflected in this place.
I simply want to say as we address this motion that we can improve our behaviour and there are ways and means of doing that. I suggest that the most appropriate way is to take responsibility ourselves and expect ourselves to behave not necessarily in ways that are nonpartisan because this is a partisan environment. We should not personalize our debates. I agree with my friend, the government House leader, when he says that we can hold strong views but we ought not to personalize our criticisms. We all agree with that but, for goodness sakes, let us not act here as though this is the corporate board room. Let us not act as though we all agree that what is going on here in terms of the various agendas and the various legislation is appropriate. There are a great deal of items the government introduces that we think are absolutely wrong. We oppose them and propose what we feel are good alternatives.
Partisanship is a reality and it should be. After all, we are elected and represent different political parties with different ideologies, platforms and philosophies. It would be a sad day if we all came in here and simply agreed with everything that the Prime Minister brought forward as the terms of an agenda.
As I say, we have to take responsibility ourselves and expect members of Parliament not to use sexist language, not to use racist language, and not to participate in obscene gestures. If that actually ever occurs again the leaders of the various caucuses should take responsibility and deal with those individuals. That is the way to deal with this. We should not ask you to enforce a particular Standing Order because we feel you do already. You make a judgment call. You are elected to serve all members of the House from all sides and are not here as a mouthpiece for the government. We feel that you do the job extremely well. As a matter of fact I have yet to recall a single media report to the contrary. There have
Government Orders
always been very laudatory comments and statements made regarding the Speaker of this House.
I want simply to conclude by suggesting that with all due respect to my hon. colleague the government House leader I think he has missed the boat totally. He thinks that by suggesting that we change the rules a little somehow this is going to change deportment in this place. It reminds me of a school teacher suggesting that people wash their hands before they have their lunch. That is fine. It is probably a good idea, but you must want to do that and it must be part of your behaviour. You do not do it simply because your teacher tells you to.
In closing I want to acknowledge that while we support the amendment put forward by the Official Opposition I want to amend that.
I move:
That the amendment be amended by adding the following words after the word "Chamber":
That the party leaders, House leaders and Whips be responsible for the comportment of their caucuses,
And by adding the following words following the word "vigorously":
That this House express its continued support and appreciation to the Speaker for his excellent guidance of this Chamber.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak in support of the subamendment tabled by the hon. member for Kamloops. First of all, I would like to join the hon. member and all members of this House in saying that we realize that the Chair has a difficult task but that we are absolutely confident that you, Mr. Speaker, in the performance of your duties, will rule fairly, and that you will strive to maintain the kind of order which I believe is essential in a House that functions properly. A Speaker must maintain order.
And now we have before us a motion about procedure which is, I would think, easy to understand and which is intended to set certain limits and impose certain rules and perhaps strenghten certain others, to make the House a more normal place and a place that from the public relations point of view is more acceptable to certain people. If we look at Beauchesne's Sixth Edition, Mr. Speaker, it is almost impossible to define specific rules on offensive accusations and sexist or other com-

Government Orders
ments made by members here in this House, from time to time, something which I totally deplore.
From the procedural point of view, Mr. Speaker, it is not easy for the Chair to put in place some kind of disciplinary system that would prevent members from using such unparliamentary and reprehensible language. I agree that the Whips, the House leaders and party leaders have an obligation to enforce parliamentary discipline among members of their caucus.
What I wanted to say to the hon. member for Kamloops is that we have a problem as far as deportment is concerned. It was Charles De Gaulle who said, as several members mentioned today, that we are elected by universal suffrage. My reason for wanting to quote Charles De Gaulle is not to use what he said as an excuse, but I think it is quite true. De Gaulle said that universal suffrage is not selective but reflective. This House is a reflection of the Canadian people. And Canadians don't like the behaviour of certain members and they don't like sexist or vulgar remarks.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether instead of using Beauchesne's and the list of expressions deemed unparliamentary that is sometimes used by the Chair, we could perhaps have an almost immediate decision in cases where a member uses abusive language, in order to deal strictly and severely with members who use language that I would call "inappropriate".
I would have a question for the hon. member for Kamloops. I have been here for 19 years. Televising the proceedings of the House and committees shows that members sometimes behave in strange ways when the TV camera is turned on them while a controversial political question, perhaps charged with partisanship, is being discussed.
I would ask him whether he does not agree that television has had an effect, I would say a dramatic effect, on debates in the House. Television has brought about changes that in my opinion have caused the climate in the House to deteriorate. In many cases, we have become TV performers. Some members have a strong oratorical tradition and are good speakers-they can steal the show. Others, like me, are not steeped in that oral tradition.
I ask the hon. member for Kamloops whether he thinks that our experience with television in this House
should be repeated in the committees. Does he think that televising committee hearings will improve debate or will it just lead to more deplorable behaviour on the part of some members?
It is important, it is a current issue, Mr. Speaker, because it concerns our public image and I would not want us to begin or leave this debate today without paying particular attention to the possibility of televising committee debates.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from my hon. colleague.
Television has certainly changed people's impressions and reflections of this institution. I do not know if I necessarily agree with him that television has changed behaviour in this House. He has the benefit of having been in the House before television and after television. I have not had that opportunity. I have only been here since television was introduced into the House. I have taken the opportunity read a lot of the old Hansards. When you read the old Hansards, you certainly get the impression that this was not necessarily a quiet Chamber, that debate was pretty tough actually from time to time.
I am not certain, based on the evidence that I have seen by looking at Hansard, that there has been a change. What has changed is that what happens here, as the government House leader has indicated, is to a certain extent in the living rooms, dens and bedrooms of Canadian homes from coast to coast to coast. I think that is the reality. People are actually watching this as it takes place today, when years ago they may have read an excerpt in some newspaper or some periodical or journal. That is a reality.
People who have spent a lot of time in this Chamber know that 99 per cent of the time spent here is very business-like. The exchanges are veiy positive. They are very respectful of different points of views. From time to time they get a little rambunctious. That probably only takes place half of 1 per cent of time, if that. That is, of course, what often gets the television coverage on the news that evening or the next day, therefore, to a certain extent people get the wrong impression. Also, people listen in on the debates.
October 23, 1991

I think back to that period when a lot of cabinet ministers were being accused of doing things and some had to resign. Again, all the people who were watching were reminded time and time again, day after day, about the misbehaviour of the cabinet ministers and how they had either been dipping into funds, inappropriately or not, were being charged with this offence or that offence, et cetera. I believe that has been part of the change.
I agree with my hon. friend that television has certainly had an impact on people's perception of the House of Commons. I do not know that it has changed our behaviour. I am not certain that we even appreciate or know that the cameras are on us as we speak here most of the time. It is to be expanded to committees, which I support. There are a lot of excellent committees and work that they do that people ought to be aware of.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened not only to the previous speaker, but to the two speakers who preceded him. I want to interject from my Olympus of being around here for 17 years going off and on that if we take the motion at face value that the hon. House leader for the Conservative Party has put forth, I want to go on record with you, Mr. Speaker, and with all members of this House to say that I wholeheartedly agree with the spirit of what he is proposing here today.
I think it is about time that we did grapple with this very important issue. Every speaker who has stood in this House so far has said, yes, there is room for improvement. One of the speakers went so far as to say that television is an entertainment medium. I would go further.
Television has become the most powerful tool for communication that we have ever devised. I believe that television is a good thing for this House. Yes, perhaps it has shown the worst aspects of what we do in here, but it has potential. It does have the potential to show us at our very best.
When we debate in here, we are the highest court of the land. I cannot imagine for example a lawyer appearing before a judge and having the lawyer and judge shout back and forth at one another. I know this is not a court of law. I know we are not just a debating society. But we
Government Orders
are after all the spokespersons for all Canadians across this land. We must always remember that.
There is a basic difference between wit and boorishness. Yes, we should comment on what we have to say. Surely, we should attack each other's ideas. We should not be attacking each other.
Some of the speakers have said that they did not come here to be polite. I do not know if they used that word. They did come here and we have come here to be thoughtful spokespersons for the people whom we represent. We owe it to them, we owe it to ourselves, we owe it to this institution and we owe it to our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do want to participate in this debate. I want to begin by saying this. This is not a new subject for the House, but I think this is a new way of addressing it.
So often we get into this debate and this issue, but we do it in a way that puts us not so much by our nature but by the nature of the debate into a position of combating one another.
What I mean by that is when we normally talk about decorum or behaviour or attitudes or heckling or something that happens in this House of Commons, it is because we are responding to the issue of the moment. In other words, there is a point of order or a point of privilege because of language or behaviour or something that has happened in the institution and as a result we are here pro and con debating those issues. As a result of that, it is often done in a moment of passion rather than a moment of reasoned thought.
What I think is distinct is that what we are doing today is discussing an issue that is important to us as individual members, is important to the collective respect that this institution has and is important to the Canadian people.
I have been listening very carefully to the debate and the discussion that has gone on. I want to say two or three things. The first thing I want to say is I listened to the remarks of the New Democratic House leader. I have to say that I am disappointed in them. I am very disappointed in them in this sense. The hon. member as I listened to him, if I could digest his argument into my own words, stood up and said that the reason that we have vulgar language, racist language, sexist language or

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
other offensive language in this House is because of the government.
My constituents do not believe that. My constituents have disagreed with me and some of the positions that I have taken on regular occasions. They also have said to me on a regular basis: "It is all of us. It is all of you. You are like a bunch of children''. They may be angry with me over my position on an issue like the GST and they want to discuss it with me in the strongest possible terms, but they also understand and were very much offended by the kazoos and the hollering and the name calling that surrounded that debate.
In other words, they understand differences of opinion and respect that, but they do not expect nor do they respect name-calling and abusive and offensive language in our relationships and our debating with one another.
I am disappointed that this is the tack that the House leader for the New Democratic Party has chosen to take.
I want to touch momentarily on the remarks of the House leader of the Liberal Party. My hon. friend is a very effective debater. He makes his case well and presents his arguments in a very thoughtful, decisive and persuasive way. But there are two or three points I want to make about his remarks.
The first one is what he said concerning the third paragraph of the particular motion we are debating and I want to quote it into the record: "Canadians have expressed alarm at the excessive partisanship and lack of decorum and civility too often in evidence in the House".
His concern was that this motion is calling on the Speaker to determine what is an acceptable or non-acceptable level of partisanship. I want to disagree and say very categorically and clearly that that paragraph does not say that. It says it is a reminder to us as members of Parliament that Canadians have expressed alarm at our excessive partisanship. It does not call on the Speaker to determine acceptable or non-acceptable levels of partisanship. It says very clearly that we as members need to be conscious of our behaviour and to behave in such a way that is not excessive. I think the Canadian public is capable of deciding what is excessive and I think in fact they are doing that on a daily basis.
Second, I was listening very carefully to my friend's arguments. For a period in his remarks he seemed to imply to me, and I think to the people who are listening to the debate, that the absence of heckling, the absence of name-calling, the absence of aggressive or offensive language, is a monotone, is boredom. It is somehow namby-pamby.
That is not the case at all. The opposite of those very things that Canadians find offensive in this institution in our behaviour is very clear, well articulated, thoughtful debate. My friend from Welland Canal just said that very clearly in the words that he expressed to this House of Commons. People do not want us calling each other names because we disagree on an issue. They want us to debate the issue. They want us to as effectively and as clearly and as strongly as we can express the two sides of the issue.
I am sure as I listen to the House leader of the Liberal Party that he understands and in fact supports the need for all of us to examine our behaviour when we participate here in this House of Commons, but I wanted to make that distinction. I do not want it in any way left on the record, either directly or indirectly, that the opposite of heckling and abusive language is somehow namby-pamby behaviour. It is not. It is very distinct and it is very different.
Third, I want to say this. Looking at both the amendment and the subamendments that have been put forward on this particular motion, there seems to be a concern that the motion before us today is somehow in some way designed to be a reflection on the Speaker, or the Speaker's ability to maintain order and decorum in this House of Commons.
I think it is very important that I address that. The words that are in the motion are words that were chosen very carefully. If anyone looks carefully at the last paragraph, it says that this House supports the Speaker's vigorous enforcement of Standing Orders 16(2) and 18 particularly, and so on and so forth.
It is an expression of support for the Speaker to maintain order and decorum in the House as the Chair of this institution, as the chair of a committee, as the chair or leader of any kind of debate or issue, it is the
October 23, 1991

role of the chair. We support that. We encourage that, and that is what we are trying to do in this motion.
The really operative parts of the motion, the most important elements that we have in front of us here today are the parts that say to us as members of Parliament: pay attention. What are we doing?
It is saying that Canadians have expressed alarm at our excessive behaviour. It says that this House recognizes disruptive behaviour and verbal interruptions including abusive language lead to a depreciated or a deprecated view and respect for the institution of Parliament and its members. In other words, the whole thrust of this motion is calling on us as individuals to reflect on our behaviour, on our language and on our attitudes.
I want to say this. I remember an experience I had when I was first elected in 1980. There is family at home, Ralph and Billie Good. Ralph and Billie have been like second parents to me. I have known them since the time of the cradle. I spent as much time at their kitchen table as I think I did my own parents. I grew up with them. Their son Ian is my best friend. We have been that way since we were born.
Something happened that I thought was very significant and I have never forgotten it. Shortly after I was elected in February 1980, in fact the first Saturday thereafter, Wendy and I went out to their place for dinner and the usual game of Rummoli. I say usual because we often did that on Saturday nights. That was something that Wendy and I did with Ralph and Billie. It was a time of fun. We had a great time together. We were friends, and we enjoyed that experience.
The first Saturday after I was elected, I had not even come down to Ottawa. I had not been sworn in yet. Albert Cooper was still Albert Cooper, a small town boy from Grimshaw. There was no change, but I went out to Ralph and Billie's that night and you know, Billy started bringing out the good china. She started putting the good china on the table. I said: "Whoa stop, Billie. I am still Albert. I have not changed. That date of February 18 has not made me any different. Please put the china away. I want what we have been eating on for the last five or ten years."
I tell you that story because I think it paints a picture of what Canadians expect and want of us. My friends Ralph and Billie, who have known me all these years,
Government Orders
just because I had become elected to the House of Commons suddenly put me in a different category. It was not a category I was comfortable with. It was not a category that I wanted to be put in, but suddenly Ralph and Billie recognized that there was something different about me. There was something special about the job I had now obtained and what they wanted to do was to put me on a little bit of a pedestal.
My point is this. When we are called to the House of Commons to debate some very difficult issues, we are not called here to be street fighters. We are not called to be a bunch of children in a playground who get our way by bullying, pushing, shoving, screaming and calling people names. That is not what they want of us.
What Ralph and Billie want of me is to act in a way that brings dignity to myself, but reflects well on my friendship and relationship to them. They want to be proud of me. That does not mean I come in here and just let everything go on around me. They want me to fight hard for the Peace River riding, for my constituency. They want me to be aggressive, but they do not want me to be abusive in my language or to call someone a name just because I disagree with them.
What they want is for me to clearly and as best I can articulate the concerns of my constituency, but not in a way that destroys the dignity or in any way demeans my political opponents. They too have been elected as my friend has just said to the highest court in the land.
We are faced with a very serious reality in this country. There has been several references made to the Spicer commission. The Spicer commission was a lightening rod for a lot of feelings and attitudes in this country. It wasn't only the Spicer commission, I think every member of this House knows that when we go home to our ridings we are told regularly that people are sick and tired of us being childish. They are not sick and tired of us debating issues in an aggressive way, but they are sick and tired of our childish behaviour. They want us to clean it up.
My argument before this House is that we have to clean it up. We are living in a time when there is very much a diminishing of respect for the House of Commons and for those of us who are members of it. And yes, it is at times very much pointed at us as individuals but very often it is pointed at us as a collective group.

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
Canadians think that the problems we face in this country today are serious problems. They know they are serious because it affects them every day. When we come in here and diminish debate by turning it into an exercise of name calling, what we are really saying is: "I can't substantively put forward your position, so therefore what I am going to do is I am going to beat down the person who disagrees with me by calling him names". It is the kind of thing we did as children in playgrounds. Do you remember the expression: Sticks and stones may break my bones but names will never hurt me? The trouble is that we tend to forget that lesson. We come in here and exercise the same behaviour.
I do not believe this is a partisan question. I do not believe there is a distinction between government minister or backbencher or members of the opposition. We are all guilty of this behaviour at one time or another. I had better say this though, Mr. Speaker, there are exceptions. There are people who have managed through very long careers in this place to maintain their dignity and to not stoop to name calling. I am not one of them. I have been here 12 years and I have on several occasions lost my temper and called people names, said things that I have later regretted. But the truth is that it did nothing for the institution, it did nothing for the debate, it did nothing for me personally and it certainly did nothing for my constituents. But what it did do was to cheapen myself in terms of my own perception and certainly in the eyes of my colleagues.
The Canadian public are now saying to us that they want us to clean it up, they want us to come up out of that level of debate and come on to a higher plain, and they are demanding it because of a number of things. First, the problems we face in the country today are serious. They feel it. They know they are serious. Second, because of the television cameras, my people see what I do today. They do not read about it in the paper two or three weeks later. They know now what I have done and so they judge me instantly. As a result of that instant judgment they want an instant improvement in my behaviour.
There is a new reality. I do not think it is as a result of television cameras, but it is as a result of that new technology. People now have much more access to us as individuals and us as an institution than they had 10, 15 or 20 years ago. Today we arrive in their living rooms on a
daily basis. It isn't what they can read, it's what they can actually see. It is not somebody describing our behaviour, it is them watching our behaviour. As a result of that, they do not blame it on anybody else but they put the blame where it belongs, which is right at my feet, and they are saying to us: Clean it up.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how much time I have left. I did not notice when I started, but now I see that I have about two minutes. The motion before us is an important motion. It is not because the words are absolutely perfect. It is not because of how we end up deciding it. It is because it allows us as individuals to do two things. First, to examine our own behaviour, that is individually as well as collectively.
Second, it affords us an opportunity to say to the Canadian people who are watching the debate, who are interested in the subject and interested in this institution, that we as people involved and elected, as my friend says, to the highest court in the land, are listening to them. We are taking them seriously.
I think it is a very important debate. I think it is a very healthy debate. As I have said, it calls on all of us to come out of that lower plane of debate to rise to the occasion, to be articulate, to put forward our arguments as best we are capable, to make our colleagues, our family and our constituents proud of us. It is not because we manage to make it on the national news tonight by calling someone a name, but because we reflected a kind of dignity that sits well in this House and makes Canadians want to aspire to be members of Parliament.
My time is up. I do want to say this. The motion before us is important. I would encourage all members of the House to support it, not only in our votes because that is secondary, but much more in terms of our behaviour. We need to demonstrate to Canadians that I have dignity or I have respect for the dignity, the ability of my friends across the aisle. That is what my constituents want to hear from me. They want me to disagree with them, but they also want me to send a message to them that says that the people who are in this House are the people who have been picked by Canadians because they can represent their concerns in the finest traditions of this institution.

I appreciate the time I have had to participate in the debate. It is important and I look forward to the comments of other colleagues.

Mr. Speaker, under comments and questions. I appreciate this is a very difficult debate and we do not want it to get out of hand. I have great personal respect for the member who has just spoken. He and I and perhaps the member for Winnipeg North all need from time to time to be put on a pedestal, given that we share certain stature. I also know him to be a fine person.
Yet, I have to say that the direction of his comments or arguments, along with the government's line of attack or line of defence in this thing, I find, and I say this with the greatest respect, personally and truly offensive because I get no sense of understanding about the nature of the offence that was committed in this House with racist and sexist comments. That is the first point.
Second, there is no sense of collective responsibility on the part of either the Conservative Party or the government for its responsibilities here.
Let me say this first. All parties, all individuals have elements of racism and sexism within us. No party has the corner on virtue. What is a test from time to time is how we collectively respond when racism or sexism comes forth. I would like to think that we as a party have tried to deal with it in various ways, but I do not hear the government accepting responsibility for its response or reaction when these things occur.
There has been no reaction by the government to the individuals, what we have seen or the public has seen, to sexist or racist comments. In fact, they are defended, not in their particular, but the individuals are defended and are still in the same place. We see no initiatives coming from the Conservative Party or the government as government for dealing with these matters or any sense of understanding about the offence that has been committed. That takes me to the second part of my comment.
The member has equated racist and sexist remarks with name calling.
Name calling against an individual is to be deplored. We all share the understanding of the need to bring that under control in this and the member's arguments that that needs to be brought under control. However, racist or sexist remarks go far beyond bringing an individual
Government Orders
into disrepute or damaging or wounding an individual or, in that sense, demeaning the whole institution by tactics of that kind. Racist and sexist comments bring a whole group in our community into disrepute and they bring groups in our community which are vulnerable into disrepute.
We see and know the impact of that vulnerability daily in the hurt that it does. So this institution, as Parliament, must respond far more effectively than it has to racist and sexist comments because we are supposed to be, as the member pointed out, the highest court in this land. If we do not get our act together, if we are not seen to deal swiftly and effectively with racist and sexist comments, if in fact the government fails to understand it and equates it with personal insults, fails to understand the damage and hurt it does throughout this whole land, then we are failing collectively as Parliament.
The government, by taking the response that it has to this, fails as government. That is not a partisan remark because, as I said at the outset, no party has a monopoly on either virtue or on sexism or racism, but it is how you respond. This government has brought itself down, I say, in the eyes of the people of Canada by its failure to respond to the remarks that have been made in this House.
I would ask the member if he would just simply at least accept, on behalf of the government, some responsibility for acting and indicate that he understands the distinction between racism and sexism on the one hand and mere name calling on the other, disreputable as that may be.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for, as I see it, two questions that I want to try and respond to.
The first question is the equation of sexist and racist comments with name calling. I am not sure that I can address that in the way that I want to. I am not sure I can express myself well enough to get across what I want to say.
I understand the hon. member's argument that there is a distinction between name calling and sexist and racist comments. I understand that. Another category is reflections on a person's faith. Those kinds of comments that lump people into groups and somehow demean those groups, I understand that. I guess my problem is, and it leads into the second question that he raised, and that is what about the government disciplining a couple of

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
members, or what about the leadership of his party disciplining a member in their party and so on.
It really boils down, I think, to this, and that has been a difficult question for me. It is not one that I was able to, in my own mind, resolve quickly. We can handle this whole issue, as I see it, in largely two ways. There are various splinters of that, but I think there are two ways.
The first way is that we can define some hard and fast rules and then enforce them. The problem with that is that you then get into all sorts of legalities and all sorts of definitions. I am not sure that that works. I expressed to someone from his party just the other day when we had a discussion about this that we could go to a rule that would say that if somebody uses sexist, racist, you could list the Charter of Rights, any of those comments, and if we were to then say that that individual should be removed as a ministerial parliamentary secretary, a critic for an opposition party, what would of course happen because of the nature of this institution is everyone would be sitting around with their little hit squads waiting, and as soon as they had an opportunity they would jump. We would have had the case of yesterday of a member saying someone is a hypocrite, us demanding his resignation as critic of that party. It might work, but the danger is that it puts a legalistic solution that can never be complete and encompassing and replaces it with something that I think is more difficult but is actually in the long term the better, and that is the question of attitude. If we as individuals in this House respect one another with the dignity and an acceptance of their quality as individuals, if we can rise to the spirit of that, then we solve our problem
I think that is what personally I want to do and that is I think we as a House need to look at.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to the member's speech. I must tell you that first of all I have a tremendous respect for his words today. I have found over the three years that I have been in the House that his actions are consistent with his words. When I listen to him, I take everything that he says with sincerity.
I want to ask the hon. member a question. It is more along a communications line. Does he not think that part of the problem that we are having in this House stems
from a frustration factor that we on this side of the House experience? When we get up each day on behalf of those in our society who are disadvantaged, and who expect us to ask specific questions, tough questions of the government in order to make the government accountable, and quite often because of the power of proper packaging, a government member-and I am not referring to the hon. member-or a minister on the front bench can stand up and give an answer to a very specific question which is nowhere close to the question being asked. What we have in this House is a government whose communication skills are superior, their packaging skills are sharp.
Quite often I have seen this government, day in and day out, manipulate the national media, buying their answers which were nowhere related to the question. I am not excusing our reaction when it becomes overly frustrated on specific questions that we ask on behalf of the disadvantaged in our country, whether they be unemployed or a business on the verge of going under. I am not questioning, we should never ever lose it. I lost it today in frustration, and I am sorry I lost it. The NDP member referred to collective responsibility. I believe that this government quite often uses the power of proper packaging as a diversion to answering specific questions that we as opposition members put forward. I would like the hon. member to address that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It would have to be a very short reply I would hope because you are over your time now, as far as questions and comments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I can get consent to answer the question, because I think it is a very thoughtful one.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will be brief. First of all in terms of the government's superior communication skills, I am very flattered by that. I would argue that the results we are seeing today bring into question that assertion. I wish we were as good as the hon. member says we are.
The hon. member raises a very good point. I want to answer it in a slightly different angle than he presented it. The hon. member raised the issue of a question by an opposition member and an evasive answer from a minister causing anger and frustration. Of course that is true. We can reverse that. We can turn it inside out depending
October 23, 1991

on what our role or action is in the House at the moment.
Frustration and anger very much contribute to our behaviour in this House. That is why the whole question of decorum becomes so important as things begin to escalate, and we have all seen it. We start off with a good discussion and maybe a very good question and an evasive answer, or vice versa. Something starts to happen. The dynamics begin. Then we see the anger start to build and build and build. Pretty soon somebody is saying something they very much regret.
I have two points. First, if we start to treat each other with dignity and respect, which is what the Canadian people want us to do, we will diminish that. Second, anger, frustration and all those emotions that we feel do not justify us behaving in a way that is beneath the dignity Canadian people expect of us. I think that is what we have to get at.
There is no excuse. I could stand up and say some very abusive things because I am angry. That does not make it right. That is the fundamental question each of us has to look at.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There is another gentleman who wants to ask a question, the hon. member for Oshawa. If it is a short, brief question, I will allow it.
I do not want any anger in this House today. I hope that the hon. member will be brief and the hon. deputy House leader will be able to resolve the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I will make it a quick one because I appreciate the member and the sincerity with which he has made his statement today.
Can he explain to me why two members in the last two weeks have said something in here that we all think was wrong and none of us could do anything about it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason is that we have had a long-standing tradition in this House that when a member rises in his or her place and apologizes and withdraws his or her remarks we accept the word of the hon. member. That has been the case for a long time. Nobody is saying that offensive behaviour is acceptable to the institution. I do not think any of us believe that. We all want to rise above that. We have a long tradition
Government Orders
and it is one that requires of us some discipline and some self-censure.
When someone in the House does something we collectively consider offensive we have some very subtle ways of sending signals concerning what we think of that behaviour. Traditionally that is the way we have resolved it in the House.
We are having a debate today and I am sure the hon. member will participate. He may have some other solutions. That is the tradition we have lived by and the one we have practised thus far in our institution.
Mr. Speaker, I will be very quick. How would this present motion solve the problem of the use of such language? Will it help prevent the use of such language?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: No, it will not. What it will do, and it is already doing it, is draw our attention individually and collectively the seriousness of the problem. Only we can solve it. That is what I think we have to do.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We will now get back to debate with 20 minutes plus 10 minutes for questions and comments.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday morning, when I read the notice of the motion that we are discussing this afternoon, I was shocked that the government moved such a motion. That morning, I told our House leader that it was incredible that the government considered presenting such a motion.
Mr. Speaker, it is hard for me to understand why the government presented such a motion, even today, even after the speech by the minister and his parliamentary secretary this afternoon.

This motion is unable, as the parliamentary secretary has just said, to deal with the problem of offensive language in this House. It simply draws attention to it. It urges the Speaker to enforce the Standing Orders of this place but is not an amendment to the Standing Orders. It does not place any additional power in the Chair. It does

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
not propose any changes to the rules to make such conduct less likely.
I regret that the government has chosen to introduce a motion like this instead of dealing with the issue in a substantive way, for example, first raising it in the committee of which the parliamentary secretary is the chairman, the House management committee, and members on that committee coming up with some ideas as to how this issue might have been dealt with in a better way.
I must say that as a relatively new member in this place, having been here only three years, I was rather surprised that it was the government House leader who put this motion forward because I think it is fair to say, and I think members on all sides would agree, that he has been a very partisan and very aggressive member of this House. I agree, and I want it on the record, that he did not storm the chair. He invited me to his office to see the tape of that incident, and I was satisfied that it was he that was sitting in his seat at the time of the chair storming incident. Since my name is now constantly referred to as a witness to this event, I want to put it on the record that I agree he did not storm the chair in the famous alleged incident.
Having said that, he has been a very vigorous debater in this House over the years and has developed a certain reputation as such. To hear him mouthing the platitudes he did today about decorum in this House was quite amazing and I was somewhat astounded.
And losing it at the same time.

The hon. member is heckling. I want to make it clear that I enjoy heckling and I regard it as very much a part of parliamentary debate. All too often we are told that, as we have heard this afternoon from the parliamentary secretary and the government House leader, heckling somehow is evil. In every case that the word heckling was used by the parliamentary secretary, and I did not check the government House leader on this, he also talked about either name calling or offensive language. That is what he said. He said we do not want heckling and name calling or we do not want heckling and offensive language. There is a big difference between heckling and either name calling or offensive language.
There is no place in this House for name calling or offensive language. I quite agree with him. However,
there is ample place in this House for heckling. Indeed it is a legitimate part of parliamentary debate and has been so as long as this institution has existed, that is for well over 900 years.
If we as parliamentarians are trying to protect ourselves from the sharp barbs and questions that come out of heckling in this Chamber then we are doing a disservice to ourselves and to our country. It forces us to realize that sometimes what we are saying is nonsense and sometimes it is not true. I am using parliamentary words to describe those statements. I am not allowed to use words that some people use on the streets of this country to describe some of the speeches in this place.
I know that some of my constituents use stronger language with me on the telephone and occasionally in a letter use words-
Speaking about your speeches?

No. They are usually describing other hon. members' speeches, not my own. However, the words are there and I hear them on my telephone or in discussion. They are on the list of words in Beauchesne's that I cannot use in this place. I respect that, and I think most members respect that and try to use words like "nonsense" instead of others that might come to mind. Members will not use the word "lying" with respect to another but will suggest that perhaps the member is not telling the entire truth or is a stranger to the truth or use some other expression which may mean something similar but not the same thing.
Language in parliamentary debate and parlance is restricted by rules, many of which are very old. Some of the expressions that are prohibited are ones that no longer cause offence when they are used, but because they are on the list they cannot be used. There are others that are not on the list that could be.
We had today the example of the Speaker ruling out of order and asking one of my colleagues to withdraw a word which has previously been ruled to be parliamentary, not unparliamentary. Yet it was causing disorder in the House and the Speaker took steps and ruled it unparliamentary. Perhaps it will appear in the list of unparliamentary expressions in the next edition of Beauchesne's. I do not know.
Not too long ago I had the Speaker rule the expression windbag unparliamentary based on an 1879 precedent. There are words that ought not be used. I do not want to

dwell on the question of words. What I want to do is deal with the principle.
I agree with the parliamentary secretary. I agree with the government House leader that offensive language of any kind has no place in this House. I agree that name calling, particularly of an offensive kind, particularly racist or sexist, is completely out of place. Indeed the incidents we witnessed in the last few weeks were completely unnecessary and most distasteful. I am sorry they happened, as I am sure is every other member of this House. They tend to bring the House into disrepute. They tend to cause Parliament to be regarded very badly by our fellow citizens. I regret that it happened.
What is the purpose of this motion other than to condemn that kind of conduct which I think all members condemn? Is the government proposing something new here today, or is it just having a debate for the purpose of purging ourselves after the recent incidents? I have not been able to figure out the motive because in the speeches of the parliamentary secretary and the government House leader there was no reference to the previous incidents except in questions. I am not sure why they raised it.
I would like to turn to Standing Order 16(2) which the motion says we support. The motion reads in part:
-supports the Speaker's vigorous enforcement of Standing Order
16(2) and Standing Order 18;
Just for the members of the public who may not be familiar with what Standing Order 16(2) says I will read it:
When a Member is speaking, no Member shall pass between that
Member and the Chair, nor interrupt him or her, except to raise a
point of order.
On its face Standing Order 16(2) prohibits heckling. It has never been interpreted that way, Mr. Speaker, as you well know. I know that on occasion, Sir, you had to interrupt me in the course of one of my speeches because the heckling was so loud you could not hear my speech. You heard no objection from me about the heckling. I frankly was enjoying myself and it did not bother me that members were heckling me.
Indeed three weeks ago I was making a speech and the din was very loud. It was difficult for me to be heard. It
Government Orders
was in Committee of the Whole. To say that I was offended or upset by the heckling would be incorrect. I was not. I do not think that the Canadian public was outraged. I certainly got no letters expressing shock or outrage from members of the public at the fact that I was being loudly heckled during the course of those remarks.
Standing Order 18 states:
No Member shall speak disrespectfully of the Sovereign, nor of any of the Royal Family, nor of the Governor General or the person administering the Government of Canada; nor use offensive words against either House, or against any Member thereof. No Member may reflect upon any vote of the House, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
On occasion we have risen in this House to object to words being used by members concerning the other place or remarks made about His Excellency the Governor General. Those have been relatively rare. I must say that the remarks have occurred on both sides of the House.
I can remember when there was a Liberal majority in the other place the government House leader using very strong language to describe the conduct of the members of the other place. I objected on occasion to some of that language. I can recall that once there was a Conservative majority in the other place, after it was stacked for the GST bill, there were objections to some of the language used by members on this side of the House in describing the conduct of the other place because it was considered that the language might be disrespectful.
It was not rude or offensive. It described in colourful terms what was going on in the other place. I do not think that it was in any sense name calling, nor was it offensive language, but it was held to be contrary to Standing Order 18 because it was disrespectful.
I do not think there is any argument in any part of the House. I am surprised that the government has moved this motion to suggest that somehow these Standing Orders have not been enforced. They are enforced.
I suggest that what we need to do is make sure that the name calling and offensive language are excised as far as possible from our vocabularies.
I discussed this issue on a television interview in my riding shortly after the two incidents occurred in this House. I told one of my constituents that the members

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
of this House are not paragons of virtue. None of us is in a position to throw stones.
The hon. member looks shocked. Perhaps he is and considers that I am. I do not know. I think it is fair to say that we are not paragons of virtue. As I said to this television interviewer in my view we represent the people who elect us here. We are part of those people. We are all the same.
Before our election we were citizens as they are. After the election we have become members of Parliament, but we are still citizens as they are. We have all their foibles and all their weaknesses, and we are at one with the people we represent in a host of ways that we cannot measure here.
One of the ways we can measure it is in our conduct and our behaviour. I suggest that we do behave very much as a group of any 300 Canadians would behave if they came into a room and started having a lively discussion about matters on which they have profound disagreement.
We have tried through our rules and practices to raise the level of the debate so that the language is perhaps different from what is used in the street. The fact of calling another hon. member by the name of his or her riding instead of by name, for example, tends to force us to avoid personal references in the way that another group might if it were brought together for this purpose.
That aside, we are ordinary Canadians. However, the standard and expectation is different because we are on television in this House and elected to serve in this place. We are expected to behave in a better way and it is a fair expectation.
I do not deny that it is a fair expectation and that is why when there are breaches of the rules, where there is name calling and offensive language, we run into difficulty. We are criticized and the place is brought into disrepute.
I agree with that criticism. It is a fair criticism and it is one that we have to answer for. To the extent that this debate may encourage us to raise our standards in this House, that is fine.
I want to turn to those standards because it has been suggested that this is a new phenomenon, that somehow things have changed in the last few weeks, the last year,
the last three or four or five years. I do not know how long the government House leader has had these feelings, but obviously he did not feel pushed or moved enough to bring in such a motion in the last seven years that he has been in government. I am rather surprised that it has suddenly come on him today that we have to have this discussion.
As I say I do not know exactly why it was prompted, unless it is in response to these incidents.
What was the situation 20 or 30 years ago? I used to come and sit in the gallery when I was a teenager and watch the debates in this House. I can remember Mr. Diefenbaker was Leader of the Opposition at the time. In fact, he was Prime Minister when I was first here and Mr. Pearson was Leader of the Opposition.
I did it too.

I remember then that the debates were exceedingly lively in this Chamber. To suggest that somehow today they have changed is simply not the case.
I can recall Question Period when members used to bang their desks. The din was often so loud you could not hear anything but desk banging. You could not possibly hear a member trying to speak above the roar.
Many members lifted the wooden tops on their desks and banged them up and down rather than just pound them with their hands and I am sure you remember this, Mr. Speaker. The noise was fantastic. There was hooting and hollering and yelling.
To say that today it is noisier or different from then I suggest is simply not true. I think that the Chamber is relatively quiet in this day and age. I think it has changed a bit. I think it has changed for the better in that respect.
Also to suggest that somehow the language in debate was different I do not think is fair. I think the language at that time was very lively. I think the exchanges were very powerful. We did not hear criticism of Parliament back then. Indeed the public speaks about those days as the "good old days of Parliament" when we had real debaters like Mr. Diefenbaker. He was regarded as a great debater, and he was a great debater. He was a powerful speaker. He could keep the House in fits of laughter.
Or fits of rage.

"Or fits of rage", as the hon. member for Halifax suggests, and it is true.
October 23, 1991

I remember when Mr. Pickersgill was a member of this House. His speeches were a brilliant example of how to use heckling to full advantage. He would stand up with absolutely no message he wanted to impart and wait for heckles from the other side in order to make up his speech and run on the heckles. He had a great time. He made wonderful speeches that were endlessly entertaining and extremely useful, cogent contributions to the debates going on at the time. He was an excellent speaker.
The hon. member for Essex East as he then was, Mr. Paul Martin Senior, was another example of a great debater who could make a mountain out of a molehill. He could create arguments out of mere nothings and make the whole thing sound as though it was a learned discourse that would well suit any professorial lecture.
I appreciate the compliments of my hon. friends. In looking at this issue from any modem perspective, we have to consider that conduct in today's House of Commons has not changed. There may be a slip here and there from one day to another, but there are also improvements and perhaps those are not noted either. While there is always room for change I welcome the government's initiative from that perspective and agree that members of Parliament have to conduct themselves with decorum. The obligation is to refrain I submit from excesses of any kind but particularly of offensive, sexist, racist language or nasty name calling.
I also recognize that members can make a mistake and say the wrong thing. I think the fact that we are able to stand up, withdraw, apologize and forgive one another is a very important part of this Chamber. If we were to carry the grudge and not recognize that people say things when they should not-and we all do it at one time or another-it would be a vindictive and nasty place.
It is tough enough now when we have our disagreements about how we conduct public policy and how we run this country, but we will make it a lot tougher if we decide that we have to fight each other because someone has made a mistake. We have to be willing as the public would be willing if they were here, to forget and forgive when the time comes.
While I respect the intent of the motion, I am surprised that it is here. I hope that the government will look favourably on the amendment that has been moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton-
Government Orders
East Richmond for the reasons explained in his very capable speech. I look forward to following speeches in this debate and possibly speaking again on the main motion.

Mr. Speaker, if I understand the member for Kingston and the Islands correctly, he is trying to make a point which I think was overlooked and deliberately so. Perhaps in the government motion we have before us there is a distinction to be made between different kinds of language. All of them in their own way contribute to what is perceived as the decorum problem in the House of Commons but not all of them are morally equal. A distinction is to be made between heckling done in good humour or a kind of informal argument which is going on off the record. This looks bad on TV partly because of the way we televise the House of Commons.
It may be a matter of personal insult which ought not to be practised but which is nevertheless a matter between individual members which can be dealt with in the traditional way of withdrawal and apology, etc. We can then get into what the government describes as abusive language.
The problem is that the government seems to think that all these things are abusive and wants to submerge within the over-all concept of abusive language what has really been the catalyst for this debate and for the concern that has been expressed in the last few weeks. That is the use of racist and sexist terms. I am glad to see that the amendments from both the Liberal Party and New Democratic Party try to address that.
In our judgment, and I want the member to comment on this, this is something which we ultimately cannot expect the House to deal with solely through the office of the Speaker. We need to be able to have accountability on the part of party leadership and caucus leadership for the behaviour of members in this regard, particularly when it comes to the use of racist and sexist language.
I would agree that this is not always easy to define. Certainly there is a difference between that kind of language which is offensive to entire groups of people, whether they be women, visible minorities or whatever, and language which is offensive to one person. This can be dealt with in that interpersonal level of withdrawal, apology, and forgiveness which the hon. member rightly

Government Orders
points out is a very necessary element of living in the House of Commons.
If the good news of the gospel is the forgiveness of sins, certainly the House of Commons is a place which depends entirely on the forgiveness of sins for its day-to-day life. If we could not begin each day anew in some degree or another, indeed hourly, then we would not be able to function at all.
I invite the member to elaborate perhaps just a bit on what the government is up to in the sense of trying to submerge a larger issue which only its members have been found guilty of, so to speak, in a way of talking about the problem that assumes that we are all equal when it comes to this kind of abusive language. I would submit that we are not.

Mr. Speaker, of course the hon. member being a minister of the gospel is far better than I talking about the benefit of sin or the forgiveness of sin. I would not presume to match his eloquence on that particular subject.
However, his comments are very well taken. I regret one thing he said, and I was very careful to avoid this in my remarks, and that was the fact that the sexist and racist comments appear to come from just one side of the House. In the last few weeks that may be true, but I suspect that if one looks at the long haul this is not something unique to one side. I do not want to throw any stones in that regard and I do not think he does either. It really does not help the debate on that issue if we do that.
I agree with him that there is an attempt to draw the public's attention to the importance of this breach of our etiquette, our rules. I think it is a significant breach and one that perhaps needs to be dealt with in some other way. That is why I said at the opening of my remarks that I wished the government House leader had sent this matter to a committee instead and suggested that it be looked at. Frankly I think that is what should be done.
I know the Speaker has a committee that is looking at it and which I presume will come up with some kind of a report as a result of its discussions. This is an informal arrangement, but it could come to the committee on
House management and be dealt with there to come up with a recommendation for a rule change.
I think I was stressing the importance throughout of the need for temperance in our dealings one with the other. While I am interested in his idea that parties have to take responsibility for the conduct of their members, I have concerns about that. I think in most cases members have to take that responsibility themselves. We as individuals have to discipline ourselves. It is not up to me to sit in my seat and wait for my House leader to turn around and tell me that I have to withdraw remarks. I think I should know when I have made a mistake and withdraw or do what is necessary to apologize to a member whom I may have offended by something I said.
I am not sure that I like the idea of shifting the responsibility to party leadership, because what does it do for independent members, for example, of this House? Does it mean that they have no restraints? I think that the restraints should be equal on every member regardless of his or her position in this House. I think the restraints ought to be imposed by the Speaker on the member or by the collective discipline of the House not by individual parties.
I do not feel that the standards should be different across the House. The standard should be the same for each one of us, and the obligation should be the same for each one.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the hon. member opposite from Kingston and the Islands.
I was glad toward the end of his dissertation he finally acknowledged the very facts of what is in the motion before us. We are talking about civility, the decorum of the House, abusive language, verbal interruptions, offensive language and gestures. I agree with him that good natured heckling is beneficial. I think it is beneficial for all of us, and I am glad that he brought that point out.
I think what the motion is trying to get at is that we as individuals-he has alluded to this-have to take responsibility for our own actions here. There have been times when I have not been proud of the actions of many of my good friends here on both sides of the House. I suspect
October 23, 1991

sometimes that yours truly has got carried away as well sometimes.
I would like to ask the hon. member opposite whether or not he thinks there could be some changes made to the methods of televising the House of Commons. Originally it started out as an electronic Hansard, so it is very confined as to the rules and regulations that are given to the camera operator. It is very confined that it must only show either the Speaker or to whom the Speaker has given the floor.
Would there be a greater understanding by the Canadian public of what is happening if we were to alter those rules so that there was more fully televised coverage of what goes on here in the House?

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in this question. I was a member of the Committee on Privileges and Elections during the last session of this Parliament and the committee made recommendations to this House for improving the broadcasting of debates of this House.

I regret that that report was not accepted. The report proposed various changes, over the shoulder shots for questioners so that the minister who the question was going to could be seen. It proposed wider angle shots of the House so that the public could see who was sitting where and might see the heckling take place. It proposed wider shots showing where the person speaking was standing in the House in relation to the other persons who were sitting in the Chamber.
All those recommendations were very sensible and I regret, as I say, that they were not adopted. I am not sure that the changes in television would alter the behaviour or demeanour of the House particularly one way or the other. It might improve it slightly, I do not know. I think it would be quite neutral, but I do feel that it would at least allow the public to realize that the heckling is an integral part of the debate and sometimes extremely worth while.
I see the hon. Minister of Supply and Services here. He loves heckling, and I enjoy his comments.
If the public could see that he was here and shouting things at me at various times, I do not think they would be offended. What the public must find very difficult is not being able to hear the comments that members make
Government Orders
when a member is speaking because of our television system, not realizing that other comments are being made except to assume that perhaps they are unkind, nasty or name calling. They are not.
In my experience, name calling is exceedingly rare. I do not recall ever having been called an offensive name except a windbag. I have to admit I was not terribly offended. It was unparliamentary, I did not mind the hon. member calling me a windbag. As the hon. member said, it was a compliment.
It was an understatement.

I think name calling is a rare event in this Chamber as all hon. members know, and I think it is unfortunate that when it does happen, it attracts such attention and makes it appear as though this is going on all the time. It is not. In my experience, it is exceedingly rare.
