speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, although I thought you might refer to me as the Minister responsible for the Status of Women for the benefit of this debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I can do that, too: Also the Minister for the Status of Women.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Really in this debate I am talking as a member of Parliament because I think this is the kind of debate where we are really talking all together about an issue that is important. I think it is important to have this debate.
Unlike my colleague from Kingston and the Islands, I guess I have been more concerned about this issue in the just over seven years since I have been a member of this House. There have been many, many times when I have sat on the back bench and cringed at the display of behaviour or language which I have seen in this House, and in many ways sort of felt powerless to do anything about it. Quite honestly, I felt very frustrated. So, I am glad we are having this debate. It is the first time that I am aware of in my seven years that we have even talked about the issue. A number of us have talked about it from all parties at different times and I think it is healthy for us as members of Parliament and for the public to be

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
aware that we are concerned about our own behaviour and that we are looking at ways to improve the credibility of this House, and therefore would hope as individuals as well.
Today I want to talk a little bit about why I really think it is important to have this debate, and why it is important to have in this Chamber behaviour that is really representative of the best we can do. Also, I would comment on the issue of sexist language and why, as a woman-and I think other colleagues may share this- sexist language is so offensive to us. I have found in discussions with not only colleagues but sometimes other people don't really understand that. Obviously it cannot be a full discussion of this issue today but there will be other opportunities, but I just want to make a few comments in that area.
The resolution, broad as it is, and I know there are some amendments that we can discuss as well on it, really reflects on the ability of all the members of this House to perform the role that I think Canadians expect of us. We all know that our country is at a crossroads and the decisions that we will be making, whether on constitutional affairs or a wide variety of issues, will determine our future as a nation. Surely the choices that Canadians make about business issues, about the economy, about our education issues, our social values, will all have an enormous impact on our prosperity. The conduct and the attitudes of Canadians in an era of considerable upheaval and concern will set a stamp upon our ability to be able to continue to promote the kind of caring and compassionate society that I think we all take such pride in.
In my mind if ever in our recent history Canadians need leadership and need examples to follow and need models of responsibility and decency in the face of the very daunting challenges that we have before us, I think that time is now.
Ill-chosen words or provocative gestures, invectives or slurs or racist or sexist remarks are just going to muddy the whole area of thought and communication. These are times when very complex issues must be analysed in detail, and I would hope in a fair and rational approach. Canadians must be able to consider all options. These are times for clear thoughts to be expressed with civility and decorum and opposing positions obviously on those issues which exist must be voiced consistent with our
democratic principles, but presented without bar room antics or invectives.
This House was created as a House to bring Canadians together. It has evolved in order to help Canadians express their aspirations and enable citizens to determine the course of events of their future. When our constituents elect us, no matter what party we represent, they entrust us with enormous responsibilities. They empower us to make choices on their behalf. In doing this they have set upon us a duty to conduct ourselves and our affairs in a way that would make our citizens proud of the high ideals that lie behind our democratic institutions, that are the very heart of our democracies. In may ways I feel that when we come here as elected persons representing Canadians, we do in some ways give up perhaps some of our freedoms because we have to behave in ways I think will ensure that Canadians can be proud of us. That applies not only in the House but in other instances as well.
This House has to represent solutions for the challenges that face us as Canadians and as members of Parliament. It should not be part of the problem. Unfortunately we have had instances in recent days where I think this House has indeed contributed to the problems that we face in society, and have not been part of the solutions.
Indeed we all know that Canadians have grown quite cynical about their elected representatives and often I find people will say that it is not you. They are not going to say it to your face but they will say it behind your back. There is this sense that somehow as a group we really do not seem to have the confidence of the public. At a time when I think that we have a very important duty to set a standard of service to the nation, Canadians all too often feel that this House is nothing but a forum for bickering and it is not very productive. That is the impression that they get. That is often conveyed to me when I go home.
At a time when Canadians are looking for leadership and vision, all too often they turn on their television sets to the parliamentary channel and they get something that relates more to invective or hostility. We have to be careful that we do not get so caught up in our lives here and we are used to it all. However, for the ordinary Canadian who turns on the parliamentary channel they are coming from a very different kind of perspective and we have to relate to their values, their way of thinking about us.
October 23, 1991

I know that all members of this House feel very passionately about the future of this country, about their own views. I think all members of this House are capable of great vision and compassionate understanding. I certainly have seen it at committee hearings. I have seen it in many of the meetings, the public hearings, I have been involved in, and in meetings I have had with colleagues in all parts of the House. There has been a lot of camaraderie and respect which often is not conveyed to the public who do not see those kinds of meetings and that kind of effort that often crosses party lines.
Therefore members of this House have to be adept in the use of language to express their hopes and their aspirations. By definition members of Parliament are supposed to be accomplished communicators. You have to be to some degree to even get to this place. We have all shared the experience of debating on the hustings and having to present our views and having to defend our views. That is part of our tradition. We have all had to stretch our ability with language to its limits in order to communicate our ideals and our visions to our constituents.
We should all be very familiar with appropriately chosen language which we use to rally people around us, our ideas, to invoke the complexity of our situations and to galvanize vision into action. Language sends very powerful signals. It also sends subtle signals and very often the subtleties or the nuance or the connotation are the most powerful tools of language.
The members I think on both sides of this House have an abiding respect for this institution and a great deal of personal experience with the power of language. Nowhere should it be more evident that the use of language in this House must be part of the solution of our ability to provide leadership. We cannot let it be part of the problem.
The problem has been, as we have seen, and we could speak of the problem from many different levels, some subtle, some overt, but as the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women and as a female member of this House, I am acutely aware of the subtle messages that our every-day language conveys. I know that often we have no intention of transmitting these messages but they are conveyed unwittingly. Nevertheless they are conveyed. We still often use sex-specific words for
Government Orders
generic purposes using a term like "mankind" rather than "humanity". We often use a double standard when using words to describe situations that are substantially similar.
I have certainly heard a male colleague described as forthright while a woman colleague might be aggressive. There is a connotation that women are supposed to behave and are labelled differently when they express their views in similar ways. I am sure my colleague from across the House would agree with that.
When you use that kind of language it divides, it excludes and sends signals that may not be consciously noticed but nevertheless plays in the back of our minds and affects our attitudes.
I know that most members of this House are aware of the subtleties of gender based language and are doing what they can to apply words that unite and include rather than divide and exclude. After all, over half of our constituents are women. As elected members we owe it to ourselves as well as to our electorate to apply language that does not subtly or subconsciously exclude over one-half of our population.
The resolution before us does not just respond to the subtleties of language. In fact, if that was all we had to deal with, I do not think we would be having this debate. There are other issues that are far from being resolved.
It is when we use words that degrade. I guess I speak in this context of women and I feel particularly strongly about words that degrade women. We send signals that it is all right to degrade women. When we call a woman a name that we would never allow anyone to use to describe someone dear to us, we condone the very attitudes which, if you take the whole spectrum, ultimately leads to violence. We do not know what all those links are but we know there is a spectrum and it includes at one end the use of sexist language. It also implies that we condone attitudes that delegate women to unequal positions in our society. Surely that is not what this House is all about.
The debates in this House in the past few months have on occasion descended into the worst kind of gutter language. I have used that phrase to describe it to the media. It is language that does more than exclude and

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
divide, it is language that tries to smash and destroy the respectability of the members of this House.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, some members of this House have been working together and talking about steps that we might take to make changes. The debate is obviously one part of that today but also some of the women members of this House have met together with the Speaker to discuss gender related issues on the Hill and specifically in this House. I hope that we are going to be able to continue that work.
I know that Mr. Speaker has been veiy helpful. He has taken a lead in this area as he has in the establishment of sexual harassment policies which have been developed for employees under his jurisdiction. I think that is very important as well.
I think those kinds of steps are good. There do need to be some changes. Earlier this day at the Association of Women Parliamentarians we discussed this issue. We brought forward some ideas that are still embryonic at this stage, discussing how the rules of this House might be changed to ensure that the penalties for the use of offensive language-we were talking specifically of sexist or racist language-might be changed.
There were real penalties, penalties that might, for example, include exclusion from the House, not just naming and going out the door but having the privileges for a period of time taken away, including even potentially a fine, the withdrawal of payment for that period of time. People would know we take these things seriously. We hope that we can, not just today but thereafter, look at this situation and see how we might be better able to send out the signals. It is preventive.
We want to prevent that kind of situation from occurring, and I think these measures are important. They indicate that we all share a responsibility for making this House a model for equality and decency in which Canadians can turn with pride.
I think in the issue of language and decorum, television was mentioned earlier. It is an important change. My hon. colleague from Kingston and the Islands said that it was no different years ago. Maybe it was not but quite honestly I do not think that is good enough.
Many years ago when I worked for the Government of Ontario, I used to go into the Legislative Assembly to watch the debates. I would go in at night. I would be appalled by the behaviour and the language that went on in that Legislative Assembly during those years. There were not many women, of course, at that time at all.
I do not think we should just say that it has always been done this way, we can just carry on. In my mind with a new generation of politicians, with more women, with more people reflecting the mixed ethnic background of our country we have to come to grips with these issues. We have to convey to the Canadian public that we will establish high standards of leadership in this House.
Some people have asked how do we describe offensive language? I thought it might be helpful if I use one example. Interestingly enough the example from the Canadian Forces of our personal harassment policy provides a definition which I think in some respects might be applied to language too. It talks about personal harassment being unsolicited behaviour by an individual that is directed at or is offensive to another individual, that is based on personal characteristics, including for example race, religion, sex, physical characteristics or mannerisms and that a reasonable person ought to have known would be unwelcome.
All of us in this Chamber like to think of ourselves as reasonable persons. I hope that we will take this issue very seriously, that we will make the changes in our own rules, in our own behaviour so that we can provide an example for the Canadian public, that can provide decorum and conduct, that we can be models to the young people of this country and provide the leadership that will ensure that Canada can be proud of its Parliament and its parliamentary representation and that we can move on to the other issues which are so important to us of having a united, a caring, a prosperous Canada which we all wish for our future.

Mr. Speaker, I must say I entirely approve of what the minister said about disciplinary measures. Expelling a member from the House for using the word "slut" or similar terms
October 23, 1991

Government Orders
doesn't really change his life. I think that real disciplinary action, such as taking away all his rights and privileges for several days, would make him think. If your pocketbook is hit, it always makes you think twice, so I think this would be a very good idea.
In fact, the Association of Women Parliamentarians of Canada intends to go ahead with the resolution we intend to submit very shortly, and the gist of it, Mr. Speaker, is that you should have more authority. When something like this happens, you should have the authority to make a decision immediately and not have to wait until the member rises in the House and says "Yes, I withdraw". You should be able to decide then and there that this person has violated the Standing Orders of the House, that this individual should be expelled from the House and that the member's privileges should be taken away.
As the House leader mentioned at the beginning of this debate, to withdraw is not enough. Words are withdrawn, but that same evening they are aired on television. It really doesn't make sense, the way the system works now, and we need something else.
Mr. Speaker, I agree it is important to discuss this motion, but it is really incredible that it has come to this, that we have to discuss this kind of motion in Parliament today. In fact, I think it is demeaning.
When I first became a member of this House, I had been practising law for 13 years, and when people were asked who they trusted most in society, in Quebec, we came third. Judges came first, then doctors and then lawyers and notaries. Now I am here, I come last, and I feel insulted because one of the reasons is this matter of unparliamentary language. Of course, it isn't the only reason why we are discredited. Journalists often report what they see, and it isn't always nice. I don't think it is just our behaviour in the House but a number of other factors as well.
Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that my time is up. I will not be able to finish what I wanted to say, but I do think that we must change the Standing Orders of the House to allow you to implicate members directly, in other words, to impose your own disciplinary measures.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the minister who is responsible for the status of women and I appreciate very much many of the comments she made. I think that it is important to acknowledge that there are many times in the House of Commons when members, for a short period of time perhaps, take off their partisan cloaks or partisan hats and do work together. We have done that on issues of concern to women, issues of concern to individual women and issues of concern to women as a whole. We have done that through all parties represented in the House of Commons. That is always a very positive step and it does happen in the House of Commons.
It is important that we reiterate the difference between a lack of decorum, which is what this motion addresses, and racism, sexism, homophobic kinds of responses that we have all heard in the House of Commons. There is a difference. Racism and sexism attack a whole segment of our society, not simply me when a sexist remark is hurled to me in this House. It gives an indication of a member of Parliament's attitude towards all women in society and that is what must be recognized when we are discussing this.
The minister and I are both mothers, we are both parents, and I think we both recognize that when you are raising children, whether it is in your own home, whether you are a teacher in a classroom, whether you are a coach of a minor league sports team, that you impart to children the message that there are consequences for inappropriate behaviour. There must be consequences for inappropriate behaviour. What we have witnessed in the last few weeks is the fact that there have not been those consequences for behaviour that the vast majority of Canadians find offensive.
I want to ask the hon. minister if she will be working within her caucus to get support for the amendments that have been put forward to this government resolution and will she herself be supporting those amendments.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have not seen the wording of the amendments so far but I will certainly look at them. I agree with you, I would like to see something that will

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
add greater definition about the consequences, whether it is offensive or abusive language, sexist, racist, behaviour or gestures. I think we have to look at the whole range of those activities.
If that necessitates changing the rules of the House, because obviously there has to be something that applies to all members whether they belong to a party or are independent, I think it has to be done that way. Each one of us, through our own caucuses deals with our situation, so we have to reflect on that within our caucuses as well.
It has never been clear, up to now it has been very fuzzy. As we said, the tradition was that you could just get up and apologize, and everybody thought that that was okay. Well, we are saying now that that is not okay, that is not good enough, because of the very messages that is sending out. I think that is the wrong message, that sometimes great parliamentary traditions need to be changed to recognize the new reality that we live in.
I am not sure if we have all the answers right now, but that is something that we need to work on. I do not see it as a partisan issue, I think it is an issue that, hopefully, all members can work on.

Mr. Speaker, I think in the past few days Canadians have seen that there is a sickness called prejudice living in the halls of this institution and in the hearts of some members. I believe that most of the time it is kept well hidden, but more and more often it escapes, sullying the reputations of this institution as well as all of ourselves.
When one female member of Parliament is ridiculed because of her gender, this is ridicule against all women in this country. When one male member of Parliament is ridiculed because of his colour-he happens to be black-all visible minorities are maligned in this country. As the only other visible minority in this House, Mr. Speaker, I really feel vulnerable.
As I am speaking I must add that I have an accent when speaking English. I wonder if one day others may be tempted to ridicule me because of my accent.
Before the temptation occurs I would like to assure all members that I have no accent in my heart.
Mr. Speaker, I was to pose the same questions as the previous member. Would she support the amendments introduced by my House leader and the House leader of
the New Democratic Party? Of course I realize that she did not have the opportunity to hear the proposed amendments, that was not her fault at all.
Therefore I would like to read the amendments because we can test the principles of an answer in answering questions if the question is posed and the answer is given at the moment. When a question is posed at two o'clock in the morning and you give an answer then you know it is an answer emanating from your heart.
Therefore I would like to read the essence of the amendment. It refers to "including sexist or racist language or gestures directed at other members either during Question Period, debate or otherwise in the Chamber". That is one fundamental essence of that amendment. Part of the New Democratic Party's amendment states that "the party leaders and House leaders will be responsible for the deportment of their caucuses".
Is the minister today prepared to tell the House, having heard the substance of those amendments, whether she believes in them and would support these amendments in a spirit of non-partisanship, as she claims? Having made a decision today will she bring that message to her cabinet and convince cabinet as well? That will be the real test of sincerity and the real test of non-partisanship.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I understand this motion it is a free vote and we are here as members of Parliament. The amendment that would specifically refer to sexist or racist language would be a good idea. The member might want to consider adding physical characteristics. The member mentioned that sometimes people are ridiculed here because of a physical characteristic or manner of speech and I find that extremely offensive. By ridiculing a person all other people like them will feel that same pain, and that seems very inappropriate. So there might be a few other examples that we might want to add.
Obviously our caucuses have to deal with this and I think that is a given. I would like to see-and I am not sure if it is possible to add to the motion at this point or if it is just going to be something we will discuss later on-that the rules of this House be studied and whatever wording created to address more appropriate responses
October 23, 1991

by the Speaker to these kinds of inappropriate behaviours.

Mr. Speaker, as I begin my remarks I want to compliment my colleagues: the hon. Minister responsible for the Status of Women, the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby and the hon. member for Saint-Hubert. I am going to be speaking a little later about the Association of Women Parliamentarians and the sense of warmth we may all be feeling as women members of Parliament today after a particularly successful meeting.
As the seconder of the Liberal amendment I would like to absolutely assure you and the Speaker of the House and the other members who occupy that chair of my full confidence in each one of you, of my respect and admiration for the Speaker of the House, and of my knowledge that some of the behaviour that we have been subjected to in the last little while is not condoned by any one of you. Mr. Speaker, you do take every measure possible to combat and order such behaviour outside this Chamber. I also fully support the New Democratic Party's amendment, particularly its reaffirmation of our support for those who hold the Chair in this House.
When I listened to the remarks of the member for Kingston and the Islands it brought back a memoiy for me when he talked about coming to this Chamber as a child. As he and I are relatively the same age we may even have been here on the same day. I remember I came as a 10-year old when Mr. Diefenbaker was the Prime Minister. Unfortunately there were no Liberal MPs in the province of Nova Scotia so my mother and I were forced to go to friends in the Conservative Party to get tickets.
I remember sitting in that gallery and watching the House and being utterly fascinated, as only a 10-year old could be, and then being a little bit-no, a lot-appalled when I saw members on both sides of the House asleep. I recall one, and I do not remember which side of the House he was on, who even had a newspaper over his face and you could hear his snores in the gallery.
That has been arrested, not to say suppressed, by the advent of television in the House of Commons and we are glad of that. That kind of behaviour is not one that any one of us would appreciate or condone, but it is not
Government Orders
nearly as offensive as that with which we have put up with in the last couple of months.
When I came to this House three years ago next month I remember saying in jest to some of my colleagues: "I feel as if I am locked up in a somewhat unruly boys' school". I meant it at the time, half in jest, wholly in earnest. Now the real downside of being locked up in a boys' school is coming to the fore and it is no longer a joke.
I support very strongly the words of the member for Kamloops who talked about this House setting the tone, in a way, for all Canadians, particularly with regard to the treatment of women, visible minorities, the physically challenged and so on. In other words, the treatment of all of us to all of us and in particular the treatment of those who deserve our best treatment.
There is a tradition in this House. We have heard about that tradition. We heard about it most eloquently from the member for Kingston and the Islands and the member for Winnipeg Transcona. When the minister, my colleague from New Westminister-Burnaby and my colleague from Saint-Hubert spoke we all agreed on one point. This tradition may have seen, at least in some part, its final days. It may be time to change this tradition to reflect what is happening in the 1990s and what we must have in the 20th century. It is sad in a sense. It is sad that we cannot maintain the British parliamentary tradition of apology and withdrawal and we will all forget it like gentlemen.
Contrary to the member for Kamloops I am not a gentleman and I am not sure I can always behave like a gentleman. I do however want to try to behave like a member of Parliament.
I am angry. I am more angry today than I have been for a long time. It has been a build up of anger over the last several months. It is not just me. Women across this country are angry. People of colour across this country are angry. They are not angry about the day-to-day interruptions. They are not angry about the normal "heckling" in this House. They are angry about sexist and racist language. They are angry about personal attacks and obscene gestures. Those kinds of behaviour are simply unacceptable. They have no place in this House and every one of us in this House knows it.

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
I am sorry. It is insufficient after having heard a sexist slur, a racist slur, or a personal attack to say an apology and a withdrawal and all is forgotten. It is not forgotten. It has festered with every one of us in this House. I suspect it has particularly festered with those of us who have over our careers had to deal with such remarks.
These comments go beyond the concept of adversarial debate. Believe me, and I imagine everyone does believe me, when I say I relish adversarial debate.
My colleague from Kingston and the Islands before talked about how he liked to be heckled. Me too. I enjoy it. In the normal course of debate I am disappointed if no one heckles me. I realize that if I was heckled today it would be pretty awful, given the subject matter because this is a very serious topic.
For example my very good friend, for whom I have great respect and admiration, the member for St. John's East, when we happen to show up in the Chamber on the same duty day we enjoy heckling each other. Over the past three years we have had some memorable, interesting and I hope fairly erudite exchanges. I can also say that neither I nor the member for St. John's East would have any problem with those exchanges being read from the pulpit of any religious institution in this land. There might be some things in the content of what I say that might bother certain religious institutions but there would be nothing in the form. This is something we all have to remember.
When we deal with the question of racism and sexism, when we deal with the problem of personal attacks, each one of us knows how much that diminishes us in the eyes of the public. Make no mistake about it, the person diminished the most is the attacker. It does not diminish the victim. Indeed it probably creates an atmosphere of sympathy for the victim. What it does in diminishing the attacker is say: "This is the kind of person who gets elected to the House of Commons".
It is not. This kind of behaviour, this kind of language comes from a very small minority. I cannot emphasize too much the fact that we have in the next little while a window of opportunity in this Chamber. That window of opportunity is for us to show, to lead as an example on a non-partisan basis, for the world at large to see that we take this extremely seriously and will in some form in the very near future come up with recommendations to show how seriously we take this.
The hon. minister mentioned the work of several other committees. One is the informal group advising the Speaker of the House on which she sits, as do I and several other members including the member for New Westminster-Burnaby. It is a fairly broad question we are looking at concerning behaviour and the treatment of women generally on the Hill. We are dealing with a number of things that we are concerned with through the good offices of the Speaker of the House.
I want to talk about this a little. Today we had a meeting of the Association of Women Parliamentarians of Canada. It is a group that for a long time a number of women in this House had worked to get off the ground. I refer particularly to the member for Vancouver East who had tried for quite a while with not a great deal of success. I want to compliment in particular the member for Saint-Hubert, who had some assistance from myself and the minister and the member for New Westminster-Burnaby. This organization came together last year. It has met. It is difficult for all of us. The women of Parliament lead very busy lives as everyone else knows, but we have managed to come together on a number of occasions and we have managed to find common ground. But today marked a watershed because the women of all four parties met, discussed this issue, and there was such a sense of mutual support, such a sense of purpose, and such a sense that we as a group must come forward to the rest of you, our male colleagues, and say the time has come to make some changes.
We talk about the tradition and, yes, traditions are to be revered and to be honoured when they are good traditions, when they are traditions whose life is still germane to both the life of this place and the life of the country.
But, some of the traditions are white male, patriarchal traditions which not only have little to do with the women who sit in this Chamber, but frankly they drive us crazy. Equally frankly, Mr. Speaker, they drive the women of the country crazy. And I think, Mr. Speaker, it is because they are crazy, and it is time to get rid of traditions whose time has passed. It is time to say that we take this seriously. It is time to say this will not be accepted in the Parliament of Canada. I accept and agree most strongly that the leader of each party and the individual caucuses have a role to play. I have no qualms

about that and no qualms about knowing that my leader and my caucus, as I am sure the others, will support this, do support this, and do what is right.
But, Mr. Speaker, because of the confidence that each one of us has in you and your confreres who maintain the order and decorum in this Chamber, it is important that the rules of the Chamber reflect reality, reflect the new realities of both this Chamber and this country. Consequently I know that when we bring forward the changes that we are looking at that we will get support.
In the meantime I support most strongly, and I hope the rest of you will as well, the amendments put forward by the hon. opposition House leader, the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, the the hon. House leader of the New Democratic Party, the member for Kamloops.
This is a very serious matter, Mr. Speaker. We all know that. The time has come to act. Let us show the people of Canada that they have elected mature, caring, and compassionate people who also reflect the views of all their constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend my colleague from Halifax for the comments she made here today. Certainly we all know that she takes a very active part in what she has just spoken about and I commend her for that.
I want to say that I believe this is a very healthy debate taking place in this House. Some people seem to think it should not have happened. Well, I tend to believe that it had to happen. I think that we have come to a situation that something had to give and whether it was the constitutional committees going cross the country, or whatever it was, it brought home to me that something is wrong here. Something is wrong in this great institution and I believe we have to make amendments and adjustments to that.
I know that over the last 20 years great advances have been made by women, by minorities, and things seem to be going along relatively well.
Somewhere along the line in recent times that seemed to come to a stop. There are groups and individuals who
Government Orders
are saying things and doing things to make it less possible for these people to continue to become equal members of society. I think this is wrong.
I for one am not the greatest person watching out for what I say. I think my colleague from Halifax would be the first to recognize that, but I honestly believe that there is room for everybody in this House.
I am certainly one who agrees that things have to change and must change. I am not just talking about the sexist and racist language or gestures within this House, but I believe that other things have to change. We are the people in Canada who are setting an example for the rest of the country.
My God, Mr. Speaker, if we cannot do it, who can? Who do we expect to come to this great institution? As the member for Kingston and the Islands said: "It is 900 years old''. I agree with him. As my colleague from Halifax has said: "I agree that heckling is part of life and public speaking". We go into our constituencies at election times. We go to halls with all of the other members from all the other parties and if you do not get heckled, then you are not in it. I agree this has to be.
When we see the sexist and racist language in this House, I am appalled by it. I say to my colleague from Halifax and I ask her this question. It is a fairly straightforward question. Why do you think these things are happening at this time in our life?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Hillsborough for his question.
I am a bit reticent because I do have a definite belief and a definite reason, but I also do not want to impute reason in people who are not here to defend themselves. I have said it before so I might as well say it here and put it on the record.
I believe that these comments are based in hate. I believe they are based in fear, in ignorance and I think that we see by history that when disadvantaged groups start to achieve a certain measure of representation and equality, some people who are particularly afraid of a loss of power react in a vicious manner. Unfortunately, I think that is the case.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to raise one point. I appreciate my colleague's speech very much and I agree with her talking about traditions.
Often traditions are used to keep people in their place. I think it is going to be often heard that: "Oh, you cannot change. That is always the way it has been done". I guess as women at the leading edge, we do not accept that. We say that there has got to be a better way of doing things.
At our meeting earlier today at the Association of Women Parliamentarians, I thought it was also interesting that we had a representative of the Senate there. Perhaps we are not supposed to talk about the other place, but they indicated an interest in undertaking similar kinds of reforms. I also heard that from some male colleagues in the Senate. Perhaps the discussion we are having here will have application there as well.
There is another issue that we have talked about informally, and I just want to raise it here as well. How do we help people, our colleagues, become aware of what is offensive, whether sexist, racist or all kinds of language. Does she think it would be hopeful? I do not think you can do a dictionary. I do not think that is the approach. Is there information or some way that we can be sure that colleagues do in fact understand, that they do not get tripped up.
Sometimes there is a difference between the French and the English language of how words can be interpreted. I find there is often a generational gap. Some words that I think are offensive or sexist, much younger women do not have the same feelings about them. I am just wondering if my colleague would have some suggestions of how we get right down to the brass tacks, what we are going to do and can do.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. minister for her questions.
I think there are a couple of things.
In my position as critic for the Status of Women, which I have frequently said, I am not just your critic, Madam Minister, but I am also the critic for these things within my own caucus and I suspect my colleague from the New Democratic Party would agree with me that we have a sort of dual responsibility. One of the things, an is said in an old Nova Scotia phrase, is that you are going to catch
more flies with honey in certain circumstances than you are with vinegar. You have to in getting these things across use a certain modicum of wit and you have to use a carrot and a stick approach.
I do not mean to sound patronizing to my male colleagues because many, many of them on all sides of the House are supportive and terrific and we would not survive in this unruly boy's school without them, but I do think that there needs to be, first of all, the absolute 100 per cent support of the caucus leadership. Second, I think that the recognition of the problem is the biggest thing we have here to deal with. Everyone who is an offender or who is a possible offender has to know what it is we are talking about, because some of them do not. They do not understand. It is not penetrating their consciousness.
A realization, a sensitization perhaps to the issues is what is necessary. How to do that, because I would not want my male colleagues in my own caucus or in any of the other caucuses to think that the women were suddenly going to herd them into a room and lecture them and rap them on the knuckles, although we might if we have to, but we have to bring this to the floor so that they understand as we understand.
We talk a great deal about language in this House in the sense of communication and the duality of this country and the importance of both languages, but there is another importance here that I think we have missed and that is that sometimes the language of men and women, be it French or be it English, is sometimes incomprehensible between one gender and the other. I think learning to bridge those gaps are what we have to do.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague for Halifax for her presentation.
I recognize this as an important topic. I am delighted it is being discussed. I recognize its importance as well. I am one of those who is tiying to understand even better than I do.
As you well know, there have been a number of incidents. During the last month there have been two particular incidents that have been in fact embarrassing to the House and many of our constituents have called us. I am referring specifically to the incidents the member for Hamilton East a well as the member for Windsor-St. Clair.
October 23, 1991

I spoke out against both incidents as quickly as I could and I was surprised at how little visibility they got in spite of my attempt to explain what had happened and to in fact condemn what had happened and certainly not in a partisan way.
Basically I had three questions for my colleague. The first one is why did this happen? The member has already attempted to address that, in fact she has been rather insightful and helpful. How and what might we do in order to try to counteract some of those difficulties? There again, the member has addressed that as well.
The third point though, and very briefly, is that I was really quite surprised that some members defended that behaviour. I do not say that unkindly or in a partisan-like kind of way. I just could not believe what I heard. Why in the world would one defend that kind of behaviour when clearly virtually everyone believes that it was despicable and wrong and mean-spirited?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will recognize the hon. member for Halifax on a very short reply to that, but I would like to recognize the hon. member for Malpeque. I think she has a question for the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I will be quite brief.
I think the answer is that when something like this happens people become defensive and understandably so. It is normal to be defensive in an indefensible position. A number of people, because this is a partisan place, because we are used to being partisan and, as I said, many of us relish in being partisan, I think seriously the people who perhaps reacted in an unacceptable manner by saying that a remark was provoked or by saying that so and so deserved it or so and so did this or so and so did that, were reacting because of the partisanship that I do not deny exists and that I think has to exist. I do not make as harsh a judgment against those people. I was angry at some of those responses. As I say I have been carrying this anger for a while, but I think it is because we all in a sense had our behaviour patterns and our nerves flicked raw by what happened. We are all so upset about it that some reactions were not the reactions that we would want. That is my belief. There could be
Government Orders
another answer, but I think that is mine and I hope it is the right one.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I want to compliment the hon. member for Halifax on her very thoughtful speech here this afternoon and I want to go on record as supporting the amendments that have been put forth.
Since 1988 when I was elected I know that many of my constituents have spoken to me about the decorum in the House, the type of behaviour that they see on television. That of course includes the sexist, racist and rude comments that they see from time to time.
I certainly agree with them. To me it seems that this type of behaviour shows a total lack of respect for other members. I think being elected to this House to represent Canadians is a real privilege and I think this type of behaviour is below the dignity of this Chamber.
We have had a lot of publicity about recent developments in the House and I think it is certainly a new low of behaviour in the House of Commons at least since I was elected in November 1988.
I want to say that I am pleased we are discussing the issue today. I think it is an important and serious issue. It is one that we need to come to grips with and have to come to grips with if this Chamber is to get the respect of Canadians back again.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to put those comments on the record.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I believe there is nothing further the hon. member would like to say. On debate, the hon. member for Crowfoot.

Mr. Speaker, let me start by saying that it is ironic that we would be having such a civil debate about the use of uncivil language in the House of Commons.
I have been here now for some 17 years. I recall when I sat in a seat somewhere near where the hon. member for Winnipeg North is sitting now. I remember the first occasion when I was not sure that I was going to be able to say what I was thinking and being rather frightened by it. I want you to know how frightened I am at this moment and it is because I might say what I am thinking.

October 23, 1991
Government Orders
This institution is in terrible disrespect and it has earned it. It has earned it not because the rules do not provide for members and how they ought to conduct themselves within the Chamber. Any member who thinks that somehow this is not one of the top issues on the minds of their constituents has not been off of this 15 acres called Parliament Hill in 20 years. Everywhere in the country people are angry at how this place is conducted from within.
What is so unfortunate about that is the other obvious fact from those of us who work here that for most of the time this place works very well. It works well in our debates for most of the time; it works well in committees and in our caucuses and in our specialized committee meetings. What does not work, what is not working and what is marinating this place in the poisonous atmosphere is the environment of Question Period.
We are having a lot of discussion in this particular debate today about sexist language and racist language. I submit to you that I do not think it is a coincidence that the examples held up took place in Question Period or right after. That one 45-minute period of the day has to be reviewed. Those books on the Table have to be opened more frequently. This Chamber has to start to pay attention to such things as the question of jurisdiction, of what ministers do you ask a question to and to make note that a question cannot be argumentative. It is in Beauchesne and Erskine May now.
I simply put to any member of the House: Name the day, name the member when you have not heard an argumentative question and compare this with other parliaments around the world. This is probably the most argumentative question place. Another rule that is in the books of this House is that a question is not to have a preamble. Often you have to hunt for the question in long preambles.
If I can go on to what I think is the most important one, it is against the rules today to impute motives. Yet ever so often, including in today's Question Period, the imputation of motives is there. That, Sir, poisons this place. It poisons this environment. It leads to results we do not want. It is Question Period where we need to focus a large part of our request for change so that the
whole place can start to develop a sense of civility and respect for one another.
Like many other members I became glued to the television set on the Thanksgiving weekend past. It is about the third time in my life that I can remember when I was so fascinated by an event on television that I spent so much time watching. The other time was the Nixon hearings and more recently the situation in the gulf. This time it dealt with the ratification of Clarence Thomas, U.S. candidate to the Supreme Court of the United States. Without any capacity to judge who was right or wrong, Clarence Thomas or Rita Hill, of all of the messages and there are many, all worthy of developing speeches about racism and sexism and so on, the one that came out so absolutely clear was the utter destructive damage of the innuendo. One of those people is not telling the truth. No other fact can be drawn from that.
We are set up two sword lengths apart, established in a combative kind of a forum. The architectural design of the House does not lead to group decisions toward proper policy making as we are set up to be combative one with another. Innuendoes fly back and forth for 45 minutes that are destructive to people and destructive to this institution.
I am one who contends that the mood that is in Canada today, the negative mood that is so far below what this country so blessed with education, resources and opportunity deserves is there because most Canadians see this place as the mirror of themselves.
This is Canada. This Peace Tower is a symbol of Canada. The House of Commons is a symbol of Canada. When it conducts itself in ways unacceptable to all, then clearly Canadians are demeaned and belittled when their chief national institution is behaving in such a way.
We have to train ourselves to debate issues and not people. I believe we must do a much better job of re-examining the present rules we have for Question Period and make sure that they are obeyed. When it comes to the question of minorities, I guess I have only a few small examples of what it is like to be in that situation. The most dramatic example was either in 1960 or 1961 when I had the lifetime privilege of being in a forum in the Cow Palace in San Francisco with 22,000 persons, almost all of whom were black. Salted among
October 23, 1991

that group were just a very few white persons to listen to an address by Martin Luther King.
I remember so clearly one part of Martin Luther King's speech when he said: "The white people ask us to wait just a little longer. We have already waited for 200 years, how much longer should we have to wait?" The whole audience rose and cheered. I was a bit like a non-Catholic in the Catholic church. I did not know whether to genuflect, sit down or stand. I did not know whether to cheer or not, I was white. I could not sit there because that would be smug.
All of a sudden I was in this dichotomy of a minority and not knowing what to do with one's sense of behaviour. Therefore most of that night I was in a three quarter crouch halfway up and halfway down trying to compromise. In my heart of hearts, I felt the cause that was being spoken for and was so supportive of the views being expressed by Mr. King.
I do not subscribe to that little adage that says: "There is so much bad in the best of us and so much good in the worst of us, that there is no need for any of us to complain about the rest of us". The truth of the matter is that this place must by the demand of Canadians revisit itself and then go and wash.
I submit that while there has been a focus today on the issues of sexist language and racial language, this House must demand that we return to those days of 15 years ago when Question Periods imposed that there would be no long preambles. It imposed that there would be no innuendo. It imposed that there would be no imputation of motives because when that takes place the environment is poisoned. The whole air of what we are about is destroyed and then we get into the personal attacks. Of course no one can excuse that and of course no one ought to be able to somehow rise and justify that it came out of the mood of the moment.
The tap root of this is that it is the mood of the moment that is causing us not to discipline ourselves.
I say that this is a matter for which I think we can go some significant distance in trying to bring about the kind of respect this institution so justly deserves and that Canadians expect. I assert that if we do not give them
Government Orders
what they are looking for, they will keep changing their members of Parliament over and over again until they get what they want. Canadians will not accept a House of Commons that behaves the way this one is at the present time and has for the last few years.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Dingwall (Cape Breton-East Richmond) moved:
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should extend
certain provisions and benefits of the Older Workers Adjustment
Program to include those many Canadians employed in the
construction industry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise with regard to this private members' motion which has particular effects in the constituency I represent in this House, Cape Breton- East Richmond.

October 23, 1991
Private Members' Business
For quite some time, individuals involved in the construction industry have been calling for the active assistance and participation of the Government of Canada in order to become part and parcel of what is known in Canada as the Program for Older Workers Adjustment.
I wish to indicate to the House what the Older Workers Adjustment Program is all about and briefly to give a chronology of the things that have happened since 1984 and to submit my arguments in summation as to why I believe the Government of Canada in concert with the province of Nova Scotia should consummate an agreement on this important matter.
The Program for Older Workers Adjustment was designed to help long service older workers across the country who have no prospects for re-employment following major, permanent lay-offs. The program acknowledges the lengthy contribution of these men and women to the development of our country.
It should be noted that this is a federal-provincial partnership. The federal government is an active participant and not a mere bystander in this particular program. Its effective date was to take place with regard to lay-offs occurring on or after January 1,1988, as being eligible for consideration.
The requirements for the older worker in order for him or her to be eligible for the program is that they must be between the ages of 55 and 64 and have been in the labour force for 15 out of the last 20 years with a minimum of 750 hours worked annually, have no alternative job opportunities, no prospects for re-employment through job training or mobility, are Canadian citizens or landed immigrants resident in Canada.
The construction association in Cape Breton, known as the Building Trades Council represents an umbrella group of the construction industry trade unions which numbers about 14 in total. For the record, I would like to share those with you: International Union of Bricklayers and Allied Craftsmen; United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America; International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers; Labourers' International Union of Operating Engineers; International Brotherhood of Painters and Allied Trades; United Association of Journeymen and Apprentices of the Plumbing Steamfitting
and Pipefitting Industiy of the United States and Canada; Sheet Metal Workers' International Association; International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Chauffeurs, Warehousemen and Helpers of America; International Association of Heat and Frost Insulators and Asbestos Workers; International Association of Bridge, Structural and Ornamental Iron Workers; Millwrights and Machine Erectors; International Union of Elevator Constructors; International Brotherhood of Boilermakers, Iron Ship Builders, Blacksmiths, Forgers and Helpers. Those are the 14 unions that come under the umbrella of the Building Trades Council.
I have had the pleasure in my term as a member of Parliament to interact with numerous individuals involved in the labour movement. However, it has been a fortunate experience for me to be able to deal with the Building Trades Council because of its presidents, Mr. Ed McNeil, Dan MacDonald and other individuals who have been associated with it over the years.
In 1984 the Conservative government was duly elected in the federal election and shortly thereafter in 1985 in a statement made by the Minister of Finance a sum of money was set aside, approximately $200 million, for a program for older workers' adjustment. Shortly thereafter this organization, in concert with myself, made representations to the Government of Canada and the province of Nova Scotia to make construction workers across the country part and parcel of this particular program. In particular I was advocating that those construction workers on the island of Cape Breton and in those particular unions become part and parcel of this plan.
Between 1985 and 1989 I have raised this issue repeatedly on the floor of the House of Commons, as my colleagues will attest to. I have asked the minister numerous questions. He has been forthcoming and said that there would be some dialogue and some negotiations between the two levels of government to see whether or not something could be consummated.
In 1990, just over a year ago, the Government of Nova Scotia indicated to the Building Trades Council that now, after almost five years of hard representations, it was coming to the view that perhaps it might be able to provide some assistance and agree to undertake with the

federal government a program for older workers' adjustment in that province.
On October 11, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour and Minister of State for Transport said: "We are not able to amend the current program for older workers immediately. Hopefully there may be some other measures that can be taken for construction workers in Cape Breton". That is where it died. Nothing concrete has been done by government representatives since it was first introduced in 1985.
Is there a need? In my district and in the adjoining districts there are approximately 4,500 individuals who are involved in the construction trades industry. Upwards of 85 per cent of those men and some women are unemployed with no prospect of retraining for meaningful jobs and no prospect for any type of employment in that particular province.
Think about it. You are 54 or 55 years of age, you have worked as a bricklayer, you have worked as a carpenter, you have worked as a labourer for 25 to 35 years, and you try to seek meaningful employment when the economy is at its knees and while 84 per cent of your colleagues are unemployed. What do you do? The hard reality is that there are no employment alternatives on the island of Cape Breton. There are no meaningful prospects of retraining for other employment. There are a good 500 to 600 individuals of those 4,500 who would be readily available and eligible for a program for older workers, yet the governments seem intent on not proceeding with that particular initiative.
There is a human face to this tragedy, a real human face. Lawyers like to talk about the Constitution and they like to talk about the provisions of discrimination, but there is no group in our society who are more discriminated against than the older worker. If you are 54 years of age and are a labourer or a bricklayer your prospects for meaningful employment with a company are basically nil, if the truth be known.
The building trades in my district put forward a number of questions to their membership. They asked whether these older workers can obtain enough work to qualify for a worth-while pension through their respective unions. The answer is no.
Can they keep up with the fast pace in the construction industry today as an older worker? The answer is no. Can
Private Members' Business
they plan some easy times in the twilight of their lives? No. Can they qualify for the program for older workers adjustment? No. Can they retrain and have opportunities for other work? No.
Can they develop a "nobody wants me, nobody cares about me" attitude? Yes. Can they become reclusive? Yes. Can they develop physical and mental problems? Yes. Can they become suicidal? Yes. Can they increase medical costs to governments, both provincially and federally? Yes. Can their life-span be shortened? Yes. Can their cherished families be disrupted? Yes.
I know many of these individuals and they are good, solid, decent, dignified citizens who in their older years want to have the advantage of having a source of income in order to provide for their families and their loved ones, to live with a measure of dignity in terms of paying their mortgage and providing the necessities of life and the amenities you and I take for granted on a regular basis.
These are not crackpot individuals, incarcerated in jails, who have abused children or other individuals. They are the individuals who are involved in minor hockey and baseball. They are the ones who go out and raise money for the Cancer Society. They are the ones who volunteer their time at fire departments. They are the men and women who add meaning to the lives of others by visiting the sick and the elderly in hospitals. They are what I would call top quality Canadians and what they ask of their governments, both federal and provincial, is to be allowed to have a sense of dignity.
The provincial government took five years and the prospect of a provincial election to understand the seriousness of their request only to have the door slammed by the Minister of Labour in Ottawa. In fairness to the Minister of Labour he made himself available to meet with the Construction Building Trades Union and it representatives, but he slammed the door on them with the facetious, specious argument that construction workers cannot be included in the program for older workers' adjustment across the country because it would be too expensive.
The Government of Nova Scotia said clearly in a letter to the Minister of Labour that if it could not be done under the existing program it would amend the program under the terms of the legislation in order to have these

Private Members' Business
individuals qualify. The Government of Canada slammed the door the third time.
I am not asking for $600 million to fund a project in a sensitive political area of this country. I am not seeking to bankroll a Crown corporation. What I am seeking on behalf of these men and these women in my district and through the island of Cape Breton is a sense of dignity for them and their families.
If the president of Petro-Canada, if the president of the Cape Breton Development Corporation or the CBC or VIA Rail can get a fat-sized bonus, upwards to $80,000 in some instances, why can't you afford to pay $1,500 to $1,700 a month for a man or a woman who has contributed 30 years of their productive life to a community?
What is the problem? The problem as I see it is one of political will, of acknowledging, of supporting those men who have made a significant contribution. They are not lawyers, they are not doctors, they are not business people. But they are good solid citizens. Is it not high time that the Parliament of Canada acknowledged that?
Instead, what do we have? We have what I believe is an uncaring government. We have the likes of the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I would love to debate that minister on the rock in Cape Breton, or in his own constituency. He had the unmitigated gall to stand in the House earlier today and on previous days in the House of Commons and make reference to Bill C-21. These construction workers in Cape Breton were told by the Government of Canada "Go talk to Dingwall, go talk to MacLellan, go talk to LeBlanc, and, if we get Bill C-21 through there is probably $100 million or so to provide a cushy pension for you".
Bill C-21 went through, with my opposition Mr. Speaker, but there are no pensions, there is no program for older workers or adjustment for the construction worker in Cape Breton.
What a mean-spirited argument to put forward to people who are in desperate need.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time is somewhat limited, but I have to say to you and to members of this House that these are the kinds of issues that make Canadians very angry, when they see the President of Canada Post
closing post offices and getting a bonus, terminating VIA Rail and getting a bonus, laying off people and getting a bonus. You work for 30 or 35 years of your life in a particular trade, contribute to your community, going to your church, contributing to your church, paying your taxes in order to educate your children, and what do you have? You have the parliamentary secretary over there talking about bingo. That is what he is talking about, bingo.
There is nothing wrong with bingo, Mr. Speaker, nothing wrong at all. That is the kind of attitude that those Canadians are confronted with by this government, and it is not fair. It is not fair. Is it any wonder the country is angry and mad, when those kinds of things can go on, when a bricklayer who may live in Glace Bay or a labourer who lives in Reserve or a painter who may live in Sydney, Nova Scotia, can not get the benefits of a program which was put down by the Government of Canada to assist those who are in real economic need.
I want to tell you again, Mr. Speaker, that it is not fair. It is not fair to those men, to their families or to the industry itself. I would hope that the parliamentary secretary would reflect on the desire to fulfil the need in his remarks and say to those individuals that "I will seriously review with the federal minister to open the door again and with the provincial minister in the province of Nova Scotia to open the door there in order to provide a pool of money and benefits for those who are involved in the construction industry".
Let us remember, 85 per cent of those individuals in the construction industry in that part of Nova Scotia are unemployed. Five hundred to 600 could avail themselves of that program today. The provincial government is on record as supporting them and wants to be a participant. It would even go so far as to amend the understanding between the federal and provincial governments in order to include them.
They are men and women who have contributed greatly to our society. There is no hope of retraining for other jobs because there are no other jobs. The need has clearly been demonstrated. If you do not believe me, Mr. Speaker, talk to your friends in the Upper House. The former premier of the province of Nova Scotia, a Toiy premier, has even alluded to and concurred in the fact there is a real need there.
October 23, 1991

I ask the parliamentary secretary in good faith with great sincerity on behalf of those individuals, will he not now do the honourable thing and open the door, proceed with negotiations and consummate an agreement which will be effective in delivering a program for older workers adjustment to the construction workers in my district, in the island of Cape Breton and elsewhere in other provinces where they may want to be negotiated.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to respond to the motion from the member from Nova Scotia. It proposes that the government extend certain provisions and benefits of the program for older workers adjustment to include Canadians employed in the construction industry.
I should mention from the outset that this program does treat the construction industry like all others.
The argument or debate that was carried forward by the previous speaker was a very emotional one. I am sure it is one that caught the attention of all the people back home and I guess that was what it was meant for. This is an emotional topic. There is not one of us in this House who would not want to see any particular program extended to take in all considerations, all groups of people.
The POWA, the adjustment program that we are speaking about, was brought in by this government, not the other side of the House. We brought it in because we recognize the problem. There is not a riding in this country that has not been affected by the lay-off of older workers. My riding is the same as yours, Mr. Speaker. I will tell you it is almost punishing for a member of Parliament to witness that in their own riding. Many of these workers cannot be retrained. They are beyond the point of being retrained.
As the member mentioned, you can see the disappearance of their livelihood, the disappearance of their whole life. We do not want to see that happen. We want to see this program continue.
The fact is that it is working very well. Can it work better? Obviously it can. At the end of the day it requires dollars to make this program work. The member mentioned the $200 million that was put into the program originally and it was put in by this government. It is a
Private Members' Business
federal-provincial program. I think the member should have mentioned the percentages and how it plays out in terms of dollars. The federal government contributes 70 per cent of the cost of that program, and we do work in co-operation with the provinces, no question about it. If there is an individual need in a particular province and they want to bring it to our attention, we are more than willing to look at it and to work with them co-operatively to solve the problem.
I want to go through the criteria for the individuals who are on that program. I think it points out very, very clearly that we are sensitive to that problem as a government. To be eligible for benefits, workers from a designated lay-off, and it is very important that I use that term-Mr. Speaker, if I could have your attention for a minute. When the gentleman across the aisle spoke every one of us over here had the respect to listen. We did not shout, we did not try to scream him down, and I would expect the same courtesy to focus on the speakers on this side of the House.
The key words are "designated lay-off". With a designated lay-off for the workers to qualify they must be between the ages of 55 and 64 at the time of the lay-off. They must have worked a minimum of 750 hours per year for 15 years of the preceding 20 years. In addition, candidates must be Canadian citizens or landed immigrants and they must have no alternative job opportunities.
One of the things that is confusing the member opposite is the fact that he mentions construction workers. He is speaking about 4,000 to 4,500 construction workers. The real problem is unemployment itself. Now, he can blame the government for that and I guess we have got to take our share of responsibility. But out of that 4,500 workers-if you could give me just a minute.
Could I get unanimous consent, Mr. Speaker, to continue?
